section: Databases and Storage Engines at Big-Tech Scale
title: Structured data: tiny records, constant changes, millisecond reads
body: Blocks, files and objects are one layer; structured data sits above them. Structured data means rows, keys, documents and graph edges that an application reads and changes one small piece at a time. For a global app with 1 billion users, that is the user profile, the friend list, the "last seen" timestamp, message metadata and payment records. These records are small, change often, and people expect to read them in a few milliseconds. That combination of tiny size, frequent updates and strict latency is what shapes database design at big-tech scale.
deeper:
The chapter climbs the stack in a deliberate order. It starts at the bottom with the storage engine, the code that decides how the bytes for rows are laid out on one machine's disk. The engine sets the price of every read and write on a single node, so it is the foundation for everything else.

From there it moves up to distributed databases: how Google, Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn, Uber, Netflix and others spread those rows over thousands of machines. Each system is examined for the problem it solved, how it works and what it costs, with a recurring question: where does the system put consistency, and what does it give up to get scale?

The chapter ends with practical design tools: sharding patterns and resharding, how secondary indexes work when data is split across shards, a comparison table of the major systems, and a decision guide showing why one company typically ends up running several different databases for different kinds of data rather than one database for everything.

quiz.q: Why do small, frequently changing records with millisecond read expectations make database design different from bulk file storage?
quiz.a: Each record is tiny and updated in place or often, so the per-operation overhead (disk writes, lookups, space for old versions) dominates cost and latency, unlike large sequential file reads and writes.

title: The storage engine: three questions that set your hardware bill
body: A storage engine is the part of a database that stores and finds data on one node. It answers three questions: where does a new write go, how do I find a key again, and how do I reclaim space from old versions? The layers above it, such as SQL, replication and sharding, mostly do not care how it works. But the engine decides the cost of every single read and write, so at big scale it effectively decides your hardware bill.
deeper:
The separation matters because it lets companies mix and match. A query layer or replication protocol can sit on top of very different engines, and the chapter later shows this repeatedly: MySQL running on InnoDB or on RocksDB, Cassandra swapping its Java engine for RocksDB, Espresso and Docstore using InnoDB underneath their own distribution layers.

Two engine families dominate. B-tree engines, including InnoDB in MySQL, PostgreSQL's heap plus B-tree indexes, WiredTiger's B-tree mode and DynamoDB's storage nodes, update data in place. LSM-tree engines, including RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase, ScyllaDB and Pebble in CockroachDB, never update in place: they write new data to new files and merge those files later.

The practical consequence is that a tiny per-operation difference, multiplied across billions of rows and millions of operations per second, becomes a difference in the number of servers and SSDs a company must buy. Meta's move from InnoDB to RocksDB, covered later, is the clearest example of an engine change reshaping a fleet.

quiz.q: Why can the storage engine decide a company's hardware bill even though SQL and replication layers ignore how it works?
quiz.a: It sets the disk cost of every single read, write and byte stored on each node; at big scale those per-operation costs multiply into the number of machines and drives needed.

title: B-tree vs LSM: update in place, or never update in place
body: Two families of storage engine dominate. B-tree engines update data in place: they find the page holding a row and change it there. Examples are InnoDB in MySQL, PostgreSQL's heap plus B-tree indexes, WiredTiger's B-tree mode and DynamoDB's storage nodes. LSM-tree engines never update in place: they write new data to new files and merge files later in the background. Examples are RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase, ScyllaDB and Pebble in CockroachDB. This single design choice drives most differences in read, write and space cost.
deeper:
Updating in place means a write goes to wherever the row already lives, which can be anywhere on disk. That produces random I/O but keeps exactly one current copy of each row, so reads are simple and predictable. The price is paid at write time and in wasted space inside partly filled pages.

Never updating in place means every write, including updates and deletes, is appended as new data. Writes become sequential and cheap in the foreground, but the same key may now exist in several files. Reads may need to look in more places, and old versions consume space until a background merge (compaction) removes them. The price is paid later, in background work and read effort.

Neither family is universally better. The chapter compares them with three measures, write amplification, read amplification and space amplification, and argues that every engine is a point in a trade-off among those three. Read-heavy transactional workloads tend to favor B-trees; write-heavy, large, cost-sensitive data on flash tends to favor LSM-trees.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental difference in how B-tree and LSM-tree engines handle an update to an existing row?
quiz.a: A B-tree finds the row's page and changes it in place; an LSM-tree writes the new version to new data and leaves old versions to be merged away later by compaction.

title: Write amplification: why 1 KB can cost your SSD 10 KB
body: Write amplification is the bytes actually written to disk divided by the bytes the user wrote. If you write 1 KB and the disk sees 10 KB over time, write amplification is 10. The extra bytes come from things like rewriting whole pages, logging, and background merging of files. High write amplification matters because it burns SSD endurance, since flash cells wear out after a limited number of writes, and it consumes disk bandwidth that could otherwise serve user requests.
deeper:
The phrase "over time" is important. Write amplification is not only what happens at the moment of the write. In a B-tree, a 100-byte row change can force a 16 KB page write, plus a write-ahead log record, plus in InnoDB a doublewrite buffer copy. In an LSM-tree, the foreground write is small and sequential, but compaction rewrites the same byte roughly once per level as data moves down the tree.

So two engines can have similar total write amplification yet very different write patterns. The chapter's point is that LSM writes, even when numerous, are large, sequential and compressed, which suits flash well, while B-tree writes are page-sized and scattered.

Write amplification also shapes capacity planning. The disk bandwidth you need is user write rate times write amplification, not just user write rate. Teams that size disks for user writes alone discover that background work, especially LSM compaction, can saturate the device and stall the database. SSD endurance budgets are one of the inputs the chapter recommends for choosing a compaction strategy.

quiz.q: Why does high write amplification hurt even when the user's own write rate is modest?
quiz.a: Every user byte becomes several disk bytes, wearing out SSD cells faster and eating disk bandwidth, so the device can saturate or wear out well before user traffic alone would suggest.

title: Read and space amplification: places to look, bytes to keep
body: Read amplification is how many disk reads, or places you must look, to answer one query. An engine that keeps one copy of each row in a known page has low read amplification; one that may need to check several files has higher. Space amplification is bytes on disk divided by the size of the live data. Old versions, deleted rows that have not been cleaned up, and half-empty pages all add space. Together with write amplification, these are the three numbers used to compare storage engines.
deeper:
These measures map directly onto the two engine families. A B-tree has low read amplification: its tree is only 3 to 5 levels deep and the top levels are cached, so a point read costs about one disk read. But its space amplification suffers from pages left 50 to 70 percent full after splits; Meta measured 25 to 30 percent wasted space from fragmentation in its InnoDB fleet.

An LSM-tree has higher read amplification because a key may live in the memtable or any of several on-disk files, which must be checked newest first. Bloom filters and a block cache reduce this. Its space amplification depends on compaction: leveled compaction keeps it low, about 1.1 times the live data, while tiered compaction lets duplicates live longer and may temporarily need double the space during a big merge.

Thinking in these three numbers turns vague claims like "LSM is faster" into precise questions: faster at what, and what does it cost elsewhere?

quiz.q: Give two sources of space amplification and explain why they add bytes beyond the live data.
quiz.a: Half-empty pages (B-tree splits leave free space) and stale versions or tombstoned rows (LSM files keep old copies until compaction) both occupy disk while holding no live data.

title: The RUM conjecture: pick two of read, write, space
body: The RUM conjecture is a useful rule of thumb for storage engines. It says you can optimize two of the three costs, read amplification, write amplification (update cost) and space amplification (memory and disk), but not all three at once. Improving one pushes cost into another. Every storage engine is therefore a point in this trade-off space rather than a universal winner. Knowing which two matter most for a workload is the first step to choosing an engine or tuning one.
deeper:
The conjecture explains why engine debates rarely end. A B-tree favors reads: about one disk read per point lookup and excellent range scans, but it pays in write amplification (whole-page writes for small changes) and space (fragmented pages). A leveled LSM-tree favors space and makes writes sequential, but pays with high compaction write amplification and more read effort. A tiered LSM-tree lowers write amplification further, but raises both read and space amplification.

Even within one engine, the knobs trace the same curve. RocksDB offers leveled, universal (tiered) and FIFO compaction, bloom filters that spend memory to reduce reads, and block caches that trade RAM for fewer disk reads. Each knob moves the engine along the RUM surface rather than escaping it.

In practice this turns engine selection into a workload question. What is the write rate per node? Are reads point lookups or range scans? Does data expire? Is space or SSD endurance the expensive resource? The answers tell you which two corners to optimize and which cost to accept.

quiz.q: According to the RUM conjecture, why can't an engine be tuned to be best at reads, writes and space simultaneously?
quiz.a: Reducing one amplification pushes work or bytes into another, such as saving writes by allowing overlapping files, which costs reads and space, so at most two can be optimized together.

title: Why a B-tree finds any row in about one disk read
body: A B-tree, in practice a B+tree, is a wide, shallow tree of fixed-size pages, often 4 to 16 KB. Inner pages hold keys and pointers to child pages. Leaf pages hold the rows, or pointers to them. Because each page holds a few hundred keys (the fan-out), even billions of rows need only 3 to 5 levels. The top levels are nearly always cached in memory, so a point read typically costs about one disk read: the leaf page.
deeper:
Fan-out is the key to the shallow shape. With a few hundred keys per page, each level multiplies the number of reachable rows by a few hundred, so three to five levels are enough to index billions of rows. Contrast this with a binary tree, which would need around 30 levels for a billion keys.

The predictability is what makes B-trees attractive for online transaction processing. There is exactly one place each key can live, so read latency is stable and does not depend on how much background work is pending. Range scans are also cheap because leaf pages are sorted and linked, so a scan reads consecutive leaves.

The fixed page size is the other side of the design. The disk and buffer pool deal in whole pages, so any change to a row means dirtying and eventually writing a full page. That is the source of the B-tree's write amplification and, together with page splits, its space overhead. Those costs are covered separately, but they follow directly from the same page-based structure that gives such fast reads.

quiz.q: Why does a B-tree over billions of rows usually need only one disk read for a point lookup?
quiz.a: High fan-out keeps the tree to 3 to 5 levels, and the upper levels are nearly always cached in memory, so only the leaf page must be read from disk.

title: B-tree write path: log first, change in memory, flush later
body: A B-tree write happens in three steps. First, append a record to the write-ahead log (WAL), a sequential file on disk; this makes the write durable, because after a crash the database replays the log. Second, find the leaf page and change it in the buffer pool, the in-memory page cache. Third, later, write the whole dirty page back to disk. The WAL lets the database acknowledge a write quickly without immediately writing the modified page in place.
deeper:
The WAL is the trick that keeps B-tree writes safe without making every commit wait for a random page write. Appending to a sequential log is fast, and once the log record is on disk the change cannot be lost: if the machine crashes before the dirty page is flushed, recovery replays the log to reconstruct it.

Deferring the page write also lets several changes to the same page be combined into one flush. But eventually the whole page, not just the changed bytes, must be written back to its fixed location on disk, and those locations are scattered across the tree, so flushes are random writes.

The same log-then-apply structure appears throughout the chapter. LSM-trees also write to a WAL (commit log) before acknowledging. DynamoDB acknowledges a write once a quorum of replicas has persisted the WAL record. Aurora takes the idea to its extreme: the database sends only redo log records to storage and never writes data pages over the network, letting the storage service build pages from the log itself.

quiz.q: In a B-tree, what role does the write-ahead log play if the machine crashes before a dirty page is flushed?
quiz.a: The WAL already holds the change durably, so recovery replays the log records to rebuild the modified pages that never reached disk.

title: The hidden price of B-trees: 16 KB writes for a 100-byte row
body: Because a B-tree writes whole pages, changing a 100-byte row can mean writing a 16 KB page. That is write amplification of about 160 for that one row, plus the write-ahead log write. InnoDB adds a doublewrite buffer to protect against torn pages, where a crash leaves a page only partly written, and this doubles page writes again. The writes also land at random places all over the tree, which was painful on spinning disks and is workable but wasteful on flash.
deeper:
The arithmetic is simple: 16,384 bytes written for a 100-byte change is roughly a factor of 160. Add the WAL record and InnoDB's doublewrite buffer, which writes each page twice so a torn page can be recovered from the intact copy, and the effective amplification for small random updates climbs further.

Randomness is the second cost. Rows live in fixed pages spread across the tree, so a stream of updates to unrelated keys dirties pages everywhere. On spinning disks every random write meant a seek, which is why this was painful. On flash, random writes are fast enough to be fine, but they are still wasteful: the device writes far more bytes than the application changed, consuming SSD endurance and bandwidth.

This is the core of the chapter's B-tree vs LSM comparison. B-tree write amplification is high for small random writes because of page-sized writes. LSM write amplification can also be high, but its writes are large, sequential and compressible, which is part of why Meta's move to an LSM engine cut bytes written to flash by 75 percent.

quiz.q: Why does updating a single 100-byte row in InnoDB cost far more than 100 bytes of disk writes?
quiz.a: The whole 16 KB page must be rewritten (about 160x), plus a WAL record, and the doublewrite buffer writes pages twice to guard against torn pages.

title: Page splits: Meta found 25-30% of InnoDB space wasted
body: When a B-tree page fills up, it splits into two pages, and those pages are often left only 50 to 70 percent full. Over time the tree accumulates this empty space inside pages, called fragmentation. Meta measured that B-tree fragmentation wasted about 25 to 30 percent of space in its InnoDB fleet. That wasted space is a form of space amplification: bytes on disk that hold no live data but still cost SSD capacity, and they also hurt compression.
deeper:
Splitting keeps the tree balanced and inserts cheap, but it trades space for simplicity. A split leaves both halves with free room so future inserts do not immediately split again. Across millions of pages this adds up, which is why Meta could measure a 25 to 30 percent space cost across a whole fleet.

Fragmentation also interacts badly with compression. Each page is compressed on its own, with its free space inside, so compression ratios are weaker than for a tightly packed, sorted file. The chapter's back-of-envelope shows the effect: 200 GB of live data in a B-tree with pages about 70 percent full needs about 285 GB before compression, while a leveled LSM-tree needs about 1.1 times the compressed size.

For Meta this became decisive once its main database moved to flash. The bottleneck shifted from IOPS to capacity, and InnoDB had three space problems at once: index fragmentation, weak compression, and 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead. Those problems motivated MyRocks, a MySQL storage engine built on RocksDB.

quiz.q: Why does B-tree fragmentation hurt compression as well as raw space?
quiz.a: Pages are compressed individually with their free space inside, so partly empty, independently compressed pages compress worse than full, sorted files.

title: What B-trees buy you: predictable reads and no compaction storms
body: Despite page-sized writes and fragmentation, B-trees remain the default for many databases because of what they return. They give excellent, predictable read latency, since each key lives in exactly one place reachable in about one disk read. Range scans are cheap because leaf pages are sorted. They come with mature transaction and locking code built up over decades. And they have no background compaction storms: there is no large merge job that can suddenly compete with user traffic.
deeper:
The absence of compaction is an underrated property. LSM engines periodically rewrite large amounts of data in the background, and if that work falls behind, reads slow down and writes may be throttled or stalled. A B-tree's background work is flushing dirty pages (and vacuum in PostgreSQL), which is steadier and easier to reason about.

Maturity matters too. InnoDB and PostgreSQL have long histories of transactional correctness, locking and tooling. That is why so many large systems keep a B-tree engine underneath even while building sophisticated distribution layers on top: LinkedIn's Espresso uses MySQL/InnoDB on its storage nodes, Uber's Docstore replicates MySQL transactions with Raft, Vitess shards MySQL, and DynamoDB's storage replicas keep data in a B-tree.

The chapter's summary table puts the best fit for B-trees as read-heavy OLTP and heavy transactions. Deletes are immediate, reads are predictable, and range scans are excellent, at the cost of random I/O and 25 to 30 percent fragmentation.

quiz.q: Why might a team choose a B-tree engine for a read-heavy transactional workload even though LSM engines use space more efficiently?
quiz.a: B-trees give predictable single-read latency, cheap range scans, mature transactions and locking, and no compaction storms that can suddenly slow reads or stall writes.

title: LSM-trees: turn random writes sequential, pay later with merging
body: The log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree) was described by O'Neil and colleagues in 1996, and Google's Bigtable (2006) made it famous in practice. Its core idea is to turn random writes into sequential writes and pay for it later with background merging. Instead of updating rows where they live, every write goes to memory and a sequential log, and is later flushed to disk as a whole sorted file. Background jobs then merge these files, discarding old versions.
deeper:
The flow of a write is: append to the write-ahead log on disk, insert into an in-memory sorted memtable, and when the memtable is full, flush it as a Level 0 SSTable (sorted string table). Level 0 files may overlap in key range. Compaction then merges them into Level 1, where files are sorted and do not overlap, and onward into larger levels, each about 10 times bigger than the one above, until the last level holds most of the data.

Reads travel the opposite way: check the memtable, then the SSTables from newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit, with bloom filters per SSTable to skip files that cannot contain the key.

The payoff is that the foreground write is cheap and sequential, and on-disk files are packed full and sorted, which compresses well. The cost is deferred: compaction rewrites data multiple times, and reads may need to consult several files. Every LSM design, from LevelDB and RocksDB to Cassandra and Bigtable, is a variation on how to manage that deferred cost.

quiz.q: Where does an LSM-tree pay for making its foreground writes sequential?
quiz.a: Later, in background compaction that rewrites data several times, and in reads that may need to check the memtable and several SSTables.

title: Memtable plus WAL: fast writes that survive a crash
body: In an LSM-tree, every write first goes into the memtable, an in-memory sorted structure, often a skip list. Because it lives in memory, inserting is fast and keeps keys in order. But memory is lost on a crash, so every write is also appended to a write-ahead log, sometimes called the commit log, on disk before it is acknowledged. If the machine crashes, the engine replays the log to rebuild the memtable, so no acknowledged write is lost.
deeper:
The pairing splits responsibilities neatly. The memtable provides ordering and fast lookups for recent data; the log provides durability through cheap sequential appends. Neither needs random disk writes.

The memtable has a size limit, for example 64 to 256 MB. When it fills, it is written to disk as one immutable, sorted SSTable, after which the corresponding log segment is no longer needed for recovery. Because the memtable is already sorted, the flush is a single sequential write of a sorted file.

The same structure appears in the distributed systems the chapter covers. Each Bigtable tablet is an LSM-tree with a memtable, a commit log and SSTables, and all of these files live in GFS, so a replacement tablet server can reopen the SSTables and replay the commit log after a failure. Cassandra likewise combines a commit log, memtable and SSTables for its local storage, borrowed from Bigtable's design.

quiz.q: Why does an LSM-tree need a write-ahead log when writes already go into the memtable?
quiz.a: The memtable is in memory and would be lost in a crash; appending each write to the on-disk log before acknowledging lets the engine replay it and rebuild the memtable.

title: SSTables: immutable sorted files with a built-in index
body: An SSTable, or sorted string table, is the on-disk file an LSM-tree creates when the memtable fills up, for example at 64 to 256 MB. It is immutable, meaning it is never modified after being written, and its keys are sorted. An SSTable contains data blocks holding the key-value pairs, an index block that says which data block holds which key range, and usually a bloom filter that can quickly rule out keys the file does not contain.
deeper:
Immutability is what makes the LSM design simple and safe. A file that never changes can be cached, copied and shared without locks, and a crash can never leave it half-updated. Updates and deletes do not touch existing SSTables; they appear as newer entries in newer files, and compaction later produces fresh SSTables that replace the old ones.

The sorted layout gives two benefits. The index block lets a reader jump straight to the one data block that could hold a key, and range scans can read consecutive blocks. Sorted, packed data also compresses well, which is why a leveled LSM-tree needs only about 1.1 times the compressed data size on disk.

Immutability also enabled Bigtable's key architectural idea. Because SSTables and commit logs live in GFS (later Colossus) and are never modified in place, a tablet server holds no durable state. If it dies, another server simply reopens the same files. Replication and durability become the file system's job, not the database server's.

quiz.q: How does SSTable immutability simplify an LSM engine?
quiz.a: Files never change after writing, so they can be cached or shared without locks, cannot be half-updated by a crash, and are simply replaced by new files during compaction.

title: Compaction: the background job that keeps an LSM-tree usable
body: Compaction is a background job in an LSM-tree that reads several SSTables, merges them in key order, throws away overwritten values and deleted keys, and writes new SSTables. Without it, the number of files would grow forever, every read would have to check more and more files, and stale versions would fill the disk. Compaction is how an LSM-tree reclaims space and keeps read amplification bounded, and it is where different LSM designs differ most.
deeper:
Merging sorted files is efficient: it is like the merge step of merge sort, reading each input sequentially and writing a single sorted output. When the same key appears in several inputs, only the newest version survives. When a key has a tombstone, a special delete marker, the old value can finally be dropped.

But compaction is real work. Each byte of user data may be rewritten several times as it moves through the levels, which is the main source of LSM write amplification. It also consumes disk bandwidth and CPU that compete with user traffic, and it can cause latency spikes, as the chapter's summary table notes.

The chapter describes several strategies. Leveled compaction, the default in LevelDB and RocksDB, keeps space low at the cost of more rewriting. Tiered compaction, RocksDB's universal style and Cassandra's size-tiered style, rewrites less but keeps more overlapping files. FIFO compaction simply deletes the oldest files for data with a time-to-live. Choosing among them is a workload decision.

quiz.q: What three problems would appear in an LSM-tree if compaction never ran?
quiz.a: File count would grow without bound, reads would check ever more SSTables (rising read amplification), and overwritten or deleted data would keep consuming disk (rising space amplification).

title: Tombstones: in an LSM-tree, a delete is just another write
body: Because an LSM-tree never updates files in place, it cannot erase a key directly. Instead, a delete is a special write called a tombstone, which says "this key is gone". The tombstone goes into the memtable and log like any other write, and reads that find it treat the key as deleted. The old value stays on disk in older SSTables until compaction reaches it and drops both the old value and, eventually, the tombstone.
deeper:
Tombstones explain several LSM behaviors that surprise people. Deleting data does not immediately free space; in fact it briefly adds a little, since the tombstone is a new record. Space returns only when compaction merges the tombstone with the files holding older versions.

They also affect reads. A lookup must find the tombstone before it finds the older value, which is why reads check files newest first and stop at the first hit. Workloads that delete heavily can leave many tombstones that reads must skip over until compaction cleans them up.

The chapter's summary table contrasts this with B-trees: in a B-tree, deletes are immediate, because the row is removed from its page in place. In an LSM-tree, deletes are tombstones until compaction. For data that naturally expires, FIFO compaction in RocksDB or Cassandra's time-window strategy sidesteps much of this by dropping whole old files at once instead of tracking individual deletes.

quiz.q: Why doesn't deleting a key in an LSM-tree free disk space right away?
quiz.a: The delete is written as a tombstone record; the old value remains in older SSTables until compaction merges them and discards both.

title: LSM reads: newest first, and why that costs extra lookups
body: To read a key, an LSM-tree checks the memtable first, then possibly many SSTables, from newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit. Newest first matters because a newer file may hold an update or a tombstone that overrides older values. Having to look in several places is read amplification. Two tools reduce it: bloom filters, which let a lookup skip files that definitely do not hold the key, and a block cache, which keeps frequently read data blocks and index blocks in memory.
deeper:
The worst case for an LSM read is a key that does not exist, or one that lives only in the last level: without help, the reader would probe every level. Leveled compaction limits the damage by guaranteeing SSTables inside one level do not overlap in key range, so a point read checks at most one file per level. Level 0 is the exception, because freshly flushed files may overlap.

Bloom filters cut most of the remaining probes by answering "definitely not here" for files that lack the key. The block cache then turns many of the remaining disk reads into memory reads for hot data and for index blocks.

Range scans are harder. Bloom filters cannot help them, and a scan must merge several sorted runs from different files into one ordered stream. The chapter rates LSM range scans as good but not excellent, compared with a B-tree's excellent scans over linked, sorted leaf pages. When compaction falls behind, more overlapping files accumulate and read amplification rises further.

quiz.q: Why must an LSM-tree check SSTables from newest to oldest when reading a key?
quiz.a: A newer file may contain a later update or a tombstone that overrides older values, so the first hit found newest-first is the correct current answer.

title: Bloom filters: 10 bits per key to skip 99% of wrong files
body: A bloom filter is a small bit array kept for each SSTable that answers one question: is this key definitely not in this file? It can say "definitely not" or "maybe". With about 10 bits per key, the false-positive rate is about 1 percent, so a point lookup skips almost all files that do not contain the key and reads only the ones that might. That turns an LSM read from probing many files into usually touching just one.
deeper:
The asymmetry is what makes bloom filters safe. They never give false negatives: if the filter says a key is absent, it is absent, so skipping the file is always correct. A false positive only costs one unnecessary block read, which at a 1 percent rate is cheap.

The cost is memory: about 10 bits per key per SSTable. That is a classic RUM trade, spending space to reduce read amplification.

The big limitation is range scans. A bloom filter hashes individual keys, so it has no way to answer "does this file contain any key between A and B?" Range queries must still consult every file whose key range overlaps. RocksDB partly addresses this with prefix bloom filters: if queries commonly scan all keys sharing a fixed prefix, such as one user's rows, the filter can be built on that prefix, letting the scan skip files that hold no keys with it. This is one of the features RocksDB added on top of LevelDB.

quiz.q: What query type do per-SSTable bloom filters not help, and why?
quiz.a: Range scans, because bloom filters test individual hashed keys and cannot say whether any key in a range exists; RocksDB's prefix bloom filters help only for fixed common prefixes.

title: Leveled compaction: at most one file per level per read
body: Leveled compaction is the default in LevelDB and RocksDB. Data is organized into levels L1, L2 and onward, and each level is about 10 times larger than the one before; that ratio is called the fan-out or size multiplier. Inside one level, SSTables do not overlap in key range, so a point read checks at most one file per level. When level N grows too big, the engine picks a file and merges it into the overlapping files of level N+1.
deeper:
The non-overlap rule is what bounds read amplification. Because each level partitions the key space cleanly, finding a key means one index lookup per level rather than checking every file. Level 0 is the exception: files flushed directly from the memtable may overlap, which is why a backlog in Level 0 hurts reads so quickly.

The merge itself is incremental. Rather than rewriting a whole level, compaction takes one file from level N and rewrites only the files in level N+1 whose key ranges overlap it. That keeps each compaction job bounded, but it also means a single file's worth of data may cause up to about 10 times its size of level N+1 data to be rewritten.

The 10x multiplier shapes the whole tree. Most data ends up in the last level, and each byte is rewritten roughly once per level on its way down. That produces leveled compaction's characteristic profile: low space amplification and good reads, paid for with high write amplification.

quiz.q: Why can a point read under leveled compaction check at most one SSTable per level (excluding Level 0)?
quiz.a: Within each level from L1 down, SSTables cover non-overlapping key ranges, so only one file per level can possibly contain a given key.

title: Leveled trade-off: about 11% space overhead, lots of rewriting
body: Leveled compaction keeps space amplification low. With a size multiplier of 10, about 90 percent of the data sits in the last level, so stale copies in the upper levels add only about 11 percent extra space. The price is high write amplification. Each byte is rewritten roughly once per level as it moves down the tree, and each merge into the next level may rewrite up to about 10 times its own size of overlapping data.
deeper:
The 11 percent figure falls out of the geometry. If each level is 10 times bigger than the one above, the upper levels together hold roughly one ninth as much as the last level. Even if every upper-level copy were a stale duplicate of last-level data, the overhead would be about 11 percent. That is why the chapter describes leveled LSM space usage as about 1.1 times the live (compressed) data.

The write cost falls out of the same geometry. With several levels, a byte written by the user may be rewritten once at each level, and the overlap between one file and the next level makes individual merges expensive. Total write amplification can therefore be substantial.

This profile makes leveled compaction the natural choice for read-heavy data where space costs money. It also explains a failure mode: during a write spike, compaction can fall behind. Level 0 and the upper levels then accumulate overlapping files, stale versions take extra space, reads check more files, and eventually the engine throttles writes.

quiz.q: Why does leveled compaction with a 10x size multiplier keep space overhead near 11 percent?
quiz.a: About 90 percent of data lives in the last level, so all upper levels together are roughly one ninth its size; even if all were stale duplicates, overhead is about 11 percent.

title: Tiered compaction: fewer rewrites, more files and more space
body: Tiered compaction is used by RocksDB's universal style and Cassandra's size-tiered strategy. Instead of keeping each level non-overlapping, it lets several SSTables of similar size pile up in a tier. When there are enough of them, it merges them all into one bigger file in the next tier. Because each byte is rewritten fewer times, write amplification is lower than leveled compaction. The cost is higher read amplification and higher space amplification.
deeper:
Reads suffer because files within a tier overlap in key range. A point lookup may have to consult several files in the same tier, not just one per level, leaning harder on bloom filters and caches.

Space suffers for two reasons. Duplicate versions of a key live longer, since they are only reconciled when a whole tier is merged. And a big merge may temporarily need double the space: the engine must write the new combined file before it can delete the inputs. Disks sized for steady-state data can run out of room during a large compaction.

The chapter's guidance is that tiered compaction suits write-heavy ingest. When the write rate per node is high and SSD endurance or disk bandwidth is the constraint, rewriting each byte fewer times matters more than the extra files and space. Cassandra, which is known for high write rates across many datacenters, offers size-tiered compaction as one of its strategies.

quiz.q: Why can tiered compaction temporarily need about double the disk space?
quiz.a: A large merge writes the new combined SSTable before deleting its input files, so both copies exist on disk at the same time.

title: FIFO and time-window compaction: let expiring data just drop off
body: FIFO compaction in RocksDB simply deletes the oldest files instead of merging them. It fits time-series or cache-like data with a TTL (time to live), where old data becomes worthless after a fixed period. Cassandra offers a time-window compaction strategy for the same reason: it groups data written in the same time window so whole windows can be dropped once they expire. Both avoid repeatedly rewriting data that is going to be thrown away anyway.
deeper:
The insight is that general compaction does a lot of pointless work for expiring data. Leveled or tiered compaction would keep merging old records down through the levels, paying write amplification, only for the records to expire and become tombstoned garbage. If data arrives roughly in time order and expires by age, the oldest file contains the oldest data, and dropping it whole is both cheap and correct.

This also sidesteps the tombstone problem. Rather than writing individual delete markers and waiting for compaction to reconcile them, the engine removes an entire file at once and frees its space immediately.

The limitation is that it only works when access and expiry are time-ordered. Data that is updated in place or deleted individually does not fit, because a single old file may still hold live records. The chapter's decision guide connects this to workloads like messages and feeds: write-heavy, time-ordered, with TTLs, often stored in Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase keyed by user and time bucket.

quiz.q: Why is FIFO compaction a good fit for TTL data but a bad fit for data updated at random?
quiz.a: With time-ordered expiring data the oldest file holds only expired records and can be dropped whole; with random updates, old files may still contain live records that would be lost.

title: Compaction style is a workload decision, not a default
body: Senior staff lens: the compaction style should not be left at its default. Choose it from the workload by asking four questions. What is the write rate per node? What is the read pattern: point lookups or range scans, fresh data or old data? Is there a TTL on the data? What is the SSD endurance budget? Leveled compaction suits read-heavy data where space costs money. Tiered suits write-heavy ingest. FIFO or time-window suits data that expires.
deeper:
Each question maps to one of the RUM costs. Write rate per node and SSD endurance determine how much write amplification you can afford: a heavily written node on consumer-grade flash may wear out quickly under leveled compaction. The read pattern determines how much read amplification is tolerable: point reads on fresh data are well served by the memtable and bloom filters, while range scans over old data depend on how many overlapping files exist. A TTL signals that most data will be thrown away, so rewriting it is waste.

The cost of getting this wrong is not only efficiency. If compaction cannot keep up with the write rate, Level 0 fills, reads slow down, and RocksDB throttles or stalls writes, turning a tuning mistake into an outage-like latency problem.

The broader lesson for design reviews is that engine defaults encode someone else's workload. At big-tech scale, where one choice multiplies across thousands of nodes, the compaction strategy is worth deciding explicitly and revisiting when the workload changes.

quiz.q: A service ingests heavy write traffic that expires after 7 days and is rarely read. Which compaction style fits best, and why?
quiz.a: FIFO or time-window compaction, because data expires by age; dropping whole old files avoids rewriting data that will be discarded, saving write bandwidth and SSD endurance.

title: Back-of-envelope: LSM stores 200 GB in far less than a B-tree
body: Take 1 billion message-metadata rows of 200 bytes each: 200 GB of live data. A B-tree with pages about 70 percent full needs about 285 GB before compression, and it compresses poorly because each page is compressed alone with free space inside. A leveled LSM-tree needs about 1.1 times the compressed size, because SSTables are packed full and sorted. Its write amplification is not small, roughly one rewrite per level, but those writes are large, sequential and compressed.
deeper:
Meta found exactly this in production. Moving its main MySQL database from compressed InnoDB to MyRocks (MySQL on RocksDB) cut instance size by 62.3 percent and cut bytes written to flash by 75 percent. Both numbers matter: smaller instances mean fewer servers and SSDs, and fewer bytes written means longer SSD life.

The reason the trade paid off is that the bottleneck had moved. On spinning disks, random I/O operations per second (IOPS) were scarce, and the B-tree's predictable reads were worth a lot. On flash, IOPS became plentiful and capacity became the expensive resource. Once capacity is the constraint, an engine that packs data tightly and compresses it well wins, even if it does more background rewriting.

The example also shows why write amplification must be read carefully. An LSM-tree may rewrite each byte several times, yet total flash writes can still fall, because B-tree writes are page-sized for tiny changes, uncompressed free space is written too, and InnoDB's doublewrite buffer adds more.

quiz.q: Why did moving from InnoDB to an LSM engine make sense for Meta once its database moved to flash?
quiz.a: On flash the bottleneck shifted from IOPS to capacity; LSM files are packed full, sorted and compress well, so they used far less space and wrote fewer bytes to flash.

title: Common mistake: assuming LSM is always faster for writes
body: Common mistake: "LSM is always faster for writes." An LSM-tree does have lower foreground write cost, since a write only touches the memtable and a sequential log. But compaction is real work that must keep up. If compaction falls behind, Level 0 fills up with overlapping files, reads slow down because they must check more files, and RocksDB will throttle or stall writes. The fix is to size disk bandwidth for compaction, not just for user writes.
deeper:
The mistake comes from measuring only the write path the user sees. In a benchmark that runs for minutes, an LSM engine can absorb writes at a very high rate because compaction has not yet caught up with the backlog. In steady state, every user byte must eventually be rewritten roughly once per level, so the sustained write capacity of the node is the disk bandwidth divided by the total write amplification.

The symptoms appear in a predictable order. First, overlapping files accumulate in Level 0 and upper levels. Space amplification rises because stale versions have not been merged away. Read latency rises because lookups check more files. Finally, RocksDB applies backpressure, slowing or stalling incoming writes to let compaction catch up. The chapter's quiz describes exactly this pattern during a write spike.

The summary table echoes it: LSM background work is compaction, and it can cause latency spikes. Planning should budget disk bandwidth, CPU and SSD endurance for compaction as a first-class workload.

quiz.q: During a write spike under leveled compaction, space use rises and reads slow down. What is probably happening?
quiz.a: Compaction is falling behind: overlapping files pile up in Level 0 and upper levels, stale versions take space, reads check more files, and eventually the engine throttles writes.

title: B-tree vs LSM at a glance: where each one wins
body: B-trees update pages in place with random I/O; LSM-trees append to a memtable and log with sequential I/O. B-tree write amplification is high for small random writes; LSM's is moderate to high but sequential and compressible. B-tree reads are predictable at about one disk read; LSM reads may need several files, helped by bloom filters. B-tree range scans are excellent; LSM scans are good but must merge sorted runs. B-trees fit read-heavy OLTP; LSM-trees fit write-heavy, large, flash, cost-sensitive data.
deeper:
The remaining rows of the comparison complete the picture. Space amplification: B-trees lose 25 to 30 percent to fragmentation, as Meta measured, while leveled LSM stays around 1.1 times the data. Background work: B-trees flush pages and, in PostgreSQL, run vacuum; LSM-trees run compaction, which can cause latency spikes. Deletes: immediate in a B-tree, tombstones until compaction in an LSM-tree.

Reading the table as a whole shows the RUM trade-off in action. B-trees buy predictable reads and scans and simple deletes, paying with write amplification and space. LSM-trees buy sequential writes and compact storage, paying with read effort and background work.

The "best fit" row is a starting point, not a verdict. Heavy transactions and read-dominated online workloads lean toward B-trees because of predictability and mature locking. Write-heavy workloads, very large datasets, flash storage and cost sensitivity lean toward LSM-trees. Meta's UDB shows the same workload can move from one column to the other when the hardware bottleneck changes from IOPS to capacity.

quiz.q: How do B-trees and LSM-trees differ in handling deletes, and what consequence does that have?
quiz.a: B-trees delete immediately in place; LSM-trees write tombstones that persist until compaction, so deleted data keeps using space and reads must skip tombstones until then.

title: RocksDB: Facebook's 2012 LevelDB fork you link into your process
body: RocksDB started at Facebook in 2012 as a fork of Google's LevelDB, tuned for fast flash storage and server workloads. It is a C++ library, not a server: you link it into your own process, and it manages the LSM-tree storage on that machine. On top of LevelDB it added multi-threaded compaction, several compaction styles, column families, prefix bloom filters, rate limiters, and many tuning knobs. Being an embeddable library is what let it spread across the industry.
deeper:
Each addition targets a real production problem. Multi-threaded compaction lets the engine use many cores to keep up with high write rates on fast flash, addressing the compaction-falls-behind failure. Several compaction styles (leveled, universal/tiered, FIFO) let teams match the engine to the workload. Column families allow separate groups of data with their own settings inside one database. Prefix bloom filters help scans over fixed key prefixes. Rate limiters cap background I/O so compaction does not starve user requests.

The library form factor is the strategic choice. Because RocksDB has no network protocol, replication or cluster management of its own, it imposes no opinion on those layers. A company can build whatever distributed system it needs and use RocksDB purely as the single-node engine underneath.

The many tuning knobs are both a strength and a burden. They make RocksDB adaptable to very different workloads, but they also mean the defaults are rarely optimal, reinforcing the chapter's advice that compaction style and related settings are workload decisions.

quiz.q: Why was RocksDB's design as a library rather than a server important to its adoption?
quiz.a: It has no opinion on networking, replication or sharding, so companies could build their own distributed layers and simply link RocksDB in as the single-node engine.

title: The engine inside the engine: who runs on RocksDB
body: RocksDB became the "engine inside the engine" for much of the industry. Meta uses it in MyRocks (MySQL), ZippyDB and many internal services. LinkedIn's Venice uses it on storage nodes. TiDB's storage layer TiKV and YugabyteDB's DocDB are built on it. CockroachDB used RocksDB and later replaced it with Pebble, a Go LSM engine inspired by RocksDB. Instagram built Rocksandra, Cassandra with a RocksDB storage engine, to reduce tail latency caused by Java garbage collection.
deeper:
The chapter's explanation is economic. Writing a correct, fast, crash-safe LSM engine takes years. Replication, sharding and query layers genuinely differ by company, because they reflect each company's consistency needs, geography and operations. The single-node engine does not need to differ. So companies build their distributed layer and reuse RocksDB underneath.

The examples show different motivations. Meta wanted MySQL compatibility with better space efficiency, so it put RocksDB under MySQL. TiKV and DocDB needed a proven local key-value store beneath Raft replication. Instagram's reason was latency: Cassandra's Java storage engine suffered garbage-collection pauses that showed up as tail latency, and moving storage into RocksDB's C++ code removed that source of pauses.

CockroachDB is the interesting counterexample. It replaced RocksDB with Pebble, written in Go, yet Pebble is still an LSM engine inspired by RocksDB. Even when a company leaves RocksDB, the design stays. The takeaway repeated in the key points: companies differentiate in replication and sharding, not in the single-node engine.

quiz.q: Why do so many companies build their own distributed database layer yet reuse RocksDB underneath?
quiz.a: A correct, fast, crash-safe LSM engine takes years to build and need not differ between companies, while replication, sharding and query layers genuinely do.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Google Bigtable: a sparse, sorted map for petabytes (2006)
body: Google needed to store petabytes of structured data, such as the web crawl, Google Earth and Analytics, across thousands of machines, and relational databases of the time could not scale that far. Bigtable (2006) is a sparse, sorted, multi-dimensional map: (row key, column family:qualifier, timestamp) maps to a value. Rows are kept sorted by row key. A famous example stores web pages under reversed URLs such as com.cnn.www, so pages from the same site sit next to each other.
deeper:
Each part of the data model has a purpose. "Sparse" means rows need not have values for every column, so wide, irregular data costs nothing for missing cells. Column families group related columns, with qualifiers naming individual columns inside a family. The timestamp dimension lets a cell hold multiple versions of a value.

Sorting by row key is the most consequential choice. It makes range scans over adjacent keys cheap and lets the table be split into contiguous ranges. The reversed URL trick exploits this: www.cnn.com and money.cnn.com would be far apart alphabetically, but com.cnn.www and com.cnn.money sit together, so all pages of one site can be read with a single scan and tend to land on the same server.

The flip side is that key design becomes the application's job. Sorted keys mean sequential keys concentrate load on one range, and hot row ranges can overload one tablet server until the tablet splits. The chapter later warns against timestamps or auto-increment IDs as the leading part of a range-partitioned key for this reason.

quiz.q: Why does Bigtable's example store web pages under reversed URLs like com.cnn.www?
quiz.a: Rows are sorted by key, so reversing the URL groups all pages of the same site together, making scans over one site cheap and local.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Bigtable's architecture: tablets, tablet servers, master, Chubby
body: A Bigtable table is split into tablets, each a contiguous row range of about 100 to 200 MB by default. Tables start as one tablet and split as they grow. Each tablet server serves roughly ten to a thousand tablets. One master assigns tablets to servers, balances load and garbage-collects files, but client data never flows through the master. Chubby, a Paxos-based lock service, holds the master lock, the root of tablet location metadata, and server liveness.
deeper:
Keeping the master off the data path is what lets one master coordinate thousands of servers. Clients locate tablets through location metadata whose root is stored in Chubby, then talk directly to tablet servers. The master only handles assignment, balancing and garbage collection, which are low-volume control tasks.

Chubby provides the coordination primitives that must be strongly consistent. Holding the master lock ensures only one master acts at a time. Server liveness in Chubby lets the master detect which tablet servers are alive and reassign tablets from dead ones. Because Chubby runs Paxos, these decisions survive individual machine failures.

Inside each tablet is an LSM-tree: a memtable, a commit log and SSTables. The files live in GFS, Google's distributed file system. Automatic splitting by size means the system grows without manual resharding, which the chapter later lists as the operator-friendliest resharding approach. The limit is that splitting reacts to growth; a sudden hot row range can overload one server until its tablet splits.

quiz.q: Why can a single Bigtable master coordinate thousands of tablet servers without becoming a bottleneck?
quiz.a: Client data never flows through the master; clients find tablets via metadata rooted in Chubby and talk directly to tablet servers, leaving the master only control tasks.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Bigtable's key idea: stateless servers over a replicated file system
body: Each Bigtable tablet stores its memtable's commit log and its SSTables in GFS, Google's distributed file system, later succeeded by Colossus. So the tablet server holds no durable state. If it dies, another server reopens the same files, replays the commit log and continues serving. This split between a stateless serving layer and a shared, replicated file system is Bigtable's key idea: replication and durability are the file system's job, while Bigtable only does indexing and serving.
deeper:
This division of labor simplifies both halves. The file system focuses on keeping bytes safe with replication across machines. Bigtable focuses on the data model, sorting, caching and serving requests, and never has to implement its own replication protocol.

Recovery becomes a reassignment rather than a data copy. When a tablet server fails, the master assigns its tablets to other servers, which open the SSTables already in GFS and replay the commit log to rebuild the memtable. No data needs to be copied from the dead machine, because none lived only there.

The immutability of SSTables makes this natural: files that never change can be shared safely by whichever server currently owns the tablet. The same pattern of stateless compute over shared durable storage reappears in later systems. Spanner stores its tablets' files and WAL on Colossus, and Aurora separates its database engine from a replicated storage service, though Aurora ships redo logs rather than files.

quiz.q: Why can a Bigtable tablet server fail without losing data?
quiz.a: Its SSTables and commit log live in replicated GFS/Colossus, so another tablet server reopens the files and replays the log; the failed server held no durable state.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Bigtable's trade-offs: single-row transactions, no secondary indexes
body: Bigtable bought scale by giving things up. It supports single-row transactions only: operations on one row are atomic, but there is no way to update several rows together atomically. It has no secondary indexes, so you can only find data efficiently by row key. Hot row ranges can overload one tablet server until the tablet splits. Even so, the 2006 paper reported Bigtable in use by more than sixty Google products. HBase is the open-source copy of the design.
deeper:
These limits are deliberate. Cross-row transactions would require coordination between tablets, possibly on different servers, which is exactly the kind of distributed work that makes systems hard to scale. Restricting atomicity to one row keeps every operation local to one tablet server.

The lack of secondary indexes pushes query design onto the application. Teams must choose row keys that match their access patterns, like the reversed URL example, or maintain their own index tables.

The hot-range limit follows from range partitioning. Sequential or popular keys concentrate on one tablet, and splitting only helps after the tablet grows or is split, not instantly.

These gaps drove Google's next system. The ads team (F1) needed SQL, strong consistency and global replication for money data, which Bigtable could not provide. That led to Spanner in 2012. Meanwhile HBase brought the Bigtable design to the open-source world, and Cassandra borrowed its LSM storage layout, combining it with Dynamo's leaderless distribution.

quiz.q: What limitation of Bigtable motivated Google to build Spanner?
quiz.a: Bigtable only offered single-row transactions (and no SQL or secondary indexes), but the ads team needed cross-row transactions, SQL, strong consistency and global replication for money data.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Google Spanner: Paxos groups plus two-phase commit (2012)
body: Bigtable gave scale but not cross-row transactions, and Google's ads team (F1) needed SQL, strong consistency and global replication for money data. Spanner (2012) splits data into tablets stored in B-tree-like files plus a WAL on Colossus. Each tablet's replicas form a Paxos group with a long-lived leader, and every write needs acceptance from a majority of replicas, often across zones or regions. Transactions spanning several Paxos groups use two-phase commit, where each participant is itself a Paxos group.
deeper:
Making each two-phase commit participant a Paxos group solves the classic weakness of two-phase commit. Normally, if the coordinator crashes mid-commit, participants can be stuck waiting. In Spanner, the coordinator is itself a replicated Paxos group, so it is not a single point of failure: another replica can take over with the transaction state intact.

Data placement is flexible. Data moves between Paxos groups in units called directories, sets of keys sharing a common prefix. A 50 MB directory can be moved in a few seconds, letting Spanner rebalance load or move data closer to its users. Directories also support entity grouping: keeping related data, such as one customer's rows via interleaved tables, together so most transactions stay inside one group.

The design was ambitious in scale: the 2012 paper describes Spanner as designed to scale to millions of machines across hundreds of datacenters and trillions of rows. It is also sold as Cloud Spanner. Its most famous component, TrueTime, is what lets these replicated, sharded transactions appear to follow one global order.

quiz.q: Why doesn't Spanner's two-phase commit suffer from a single point of failure at the coordinator?
quiz.a: Each participant, including the coordinator, is itself a Paxos-replicated group, so if one machine fails another replica continues with the transaction state.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: TrueTime: a clock that admits it is uncertain
body: TrueTime is Spanner's clock API. Instead of returning a single time, it returns an interval [earliest, latest] that is guaranteed to contain the true current time. Google keeps this interval small by installing GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each datacenter. In production, the uncertainty, called epsilon, followed a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms and was about 4 ms most of the time. Knowing exactly how uncertain the clock is lets Spanner order transactions globally.
deeper:
Ordinary server clocks drift and can be wrong by unknown amounts, which makes timestamps from different machines unsafe to compare. TrueTime turns that unknown error into a known bound. If two intervals do not overlap, their order is certain. If they overlap, Spanner knows it must wait until the uncertainty passes.

The sawtooth shape reflects how clocks are corrected: uncertainty grows as local clocks drift between synchronizations with the GPS and atomic time masters, then drops back when they resynchronize. Keeping epsilon to a few milliseconds is essential because Spanner's commit wait is set by the uncertainty: the leader must wait it out, so a larger epsilon would directly slow every write.

The hardware requirement is also Spanner's main barrier to imitation. Open systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB copy Spanner's architecture of ranges replicated by consensus plus distributed transactions, but without atomic clocks they rely on hybrid logical clocks and bounded clock skew, sometimes retrying reads that fall in an uncertainty window.

quiz.q: Why does TrueTime return an interval instead of a single timestamp?
quiz.a: Clocks are never perfectly accurate; the interval gives a guaranteed bound on the true time, so Spanner knows when ordering is certain and how long to wait when it is not.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Commit wait: how Spanner acts as if there were one global clock
body: Spanner gives each transaction a commit timestamp, then the leader waits out TrueTime's uncertainty, called commit wait, before making the write visible. After the wait, the commit timestamp is definitely in the past on every clock. The result is external consistency: if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts in real time, T1's timestamp is smaller. The database behaves as if there were one global clock, the strongest practical guarantee. It also enables lock-free, consistent snapshot reads at any timestamp.
deeper:
Without commit wait, a transaction could commit with a timestamp that another machine's clock has not reached yet. A later transaction starting elsewhere could then receive a smaller timestamp than one that already committed, and the database's order would contradict real time. Commit wait closes that gap by waiting until every clock in the system must have passed the commit timestamp.

The guarantee pays off for reads. Because timestamps faithfully reflect real-time order, any timestamp defines a consistent snapshot of the whole database. A read at timestamp T can proceed without taking locks, since everything committed before T is visible and nothing after it is. That makes large consistent reads, backups and analytics cheap.

The cost is latency. Every write pays a Paxos round trip plus a few milliseconds of commit wait, and cross-region Paxos groups make writes cost tens of milliseconds. The chapter summarizes it plainly: you buy correctness with latency and special hardware. For money data, as in Google's ads system, that is a price worth paying.

quiz.q: Explain Spanner's commit wait and what would go wrong without it.
quiz.a: The leader waits until TrueTime guarantees the commit timestamp has passed on all clocks before exposing the write; without it, a later transaction elsewhere could get a smaller timestamp, breaking external consistency.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Spanner's price and its open-source imitators
body: Spanner's correctness is not free. Every write pays a Paxos round trip to a majority of replicas plus a few milliseconds of commit wait. When a Paxos group spans regions, writes cost tens of milliseconds. You buy correctness with latency and special hardware. In industry, Spanner was designed for millions of machines, hundreds of datacenters and trillions of rows (2012 paper), and is sold as Cloud Spanner. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB copy its design using hybrid logical clocks instead of atomic clocks.
deeper:
The latency numbers follow from physics. A majority of replicas across regions means at least one round trip across long distances for every write, and commit wait adds roughly the clock uncertainty on top. Applications built on Spanner must accept that writes are slower than in a single-machine database, in exchange for never seeing anomalies.

The open-source copies keep the core pattern: the key space split into ranges, each range replicated by consensus, and a transaction layer coordinating multi-range writes. What they cannot copy cheaply is TrueTime's hardware. Instead they use hybrid logical clocks, which combine physical time with logical counters, and assume clock skew between machines stays under a configured bound. When a read's timestamp falls within that uncertainty window, they may need to retry the read.

TiDB takes a third path: a central timestamp oracle in its Placement Driver hands out timestamps. That is simple and correct but adds a round trip to one service. The choice of clock is the main thing that differs between the NewSQL systems.

quiz.q: How do CockroachDB and YugabyteDB approximate Spanner's design without atomic clocks, and what do they give up?
quiz.a: They use hybrid logical clocks and assume bounded clock skew, so they must sometimes retry reads that fall inside the clock uncertainty window.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Amazon Dynamo (2007): built so the shopping cart is always writable
body: Dynamo, described at SOSP 2007, was Amazon's internal key-value store for things like the shopping cart. Its design goal was "always writable": a customer must be able to add to the cart even during failures. It spread keys with consistent hashing using virtual nodes, and let each application tune quorums (N, R, W): N replicas, with R needed for a read and W for a write. A common setting was (3, 2, 2). Its SLA was measured at the 99.9th percentile, for example 300 ms.
deeper:
Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring, so adding or removing a node only moves the keys adjacent to it rather than reshuffling everything. Virtual nodes give each physical machine many positions on the ring, spreading load more evenly and letting machines of different sizes take different shares.

With (3, 2, 2), each key has three replicas, a write succeeds when two acknowledge, and a read consults two. Because R plus W exceeds N, a read normally overlaps at least one replica that saw the latest write. Lowering W or R trades that overlap for availability and latency.

Measuring the SLA at the 99.9th percentile rather than the average was notable: it means nearly every customer, not just a typical one, must get a fast response. Dynamo also used pluggable local engines, Berkeley DB or MySQL, underlining that its innovation was in distribution, not storage. Dynamo was leaderless and eventually consistent, and Cassandra and Riak later copied this model.

quiz.q: With Dynamo's common (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2) setting, why does a read usually see the latest write?
quiz.a: Since R + W (4) exceeds N (3), the two replicas read must overlap at least one of the two replicas that acknowledged the write.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Dynamo's failure tricks: sloppy quorums, vector clocks, Merkle trees
body: To stay writable during failures, Dynamo used a sloppy quorum with hinted handoff: if a replica is down, the write goes to another node that holds the data temporarily and hands it back when the replica recovers. Because different nodes might accept conflicting writes, Dynamo tracked versions with vector clocks to detect conflicts. The application then merged them, for example by taking the union of two shopping carts. Merkle trees were used for anti-entropy repair, finding and fixing replicas that had drifted apart.
deeper:
Each technique trades consistency for availability. A strict quorum would reject writes when too many of a key's home replicas were down. A sloppy quorum instead counts whatever healthy nodes are available, so the cart stays writable, at the cost that replicas temporarily disagree.

Vector clocks record which node has seen which updates, so the system can tell whether one version supersedes another or whether they diverged concurrently. Dynamo did not pick a winner itself; it returned conflicting versions to the application. For a shopping cart, a union is a sensible merge: an item added on either side is kept, though a deleted item can occasionally reappear.

Merkle trees make repair efficient. Each replica builds a hash tree over its key ranges; comparing root hashes reveals whether ranges differ, and descending the tree narrows the difference to the specific keys without transferring all data. Anti-entropy repair of this kind remains operationally important; Uber's 2023 Cassandra post lists slow anti-entropy repair as a main pain point, which it fixed with a repair scheduler inside Cassandra.

quiz.q: Why did Dynamo push conflict resolution to the application, and how did the shopping cart resolve conflicts?
quiz.a: Staying always writable meant replicas could accept concurrent conflicting writes; vector clocks detected them and the application merged, e.g. taking the union of two carts.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: DynamoDB is not Dynamo: leaders, Multi-Paxos and B-trees
body: DynamoDB (launched 2012, described in a USENIX ATC 2022 paper) kept Dynamo's name and its goal of predictable performance, but changed the core design. Tables are split into partitions, each with three replicas in three Availability Zones. The replicas form a Multi-Paxos replication group, and only the leader accepts writes and strongly consistent reads. So DynamoDB is leader-based and strongly consistent within a partition. It is not a Dynamo-style leaderless, eventually consistent system, despite the shared name.
deeper:
The differences are concrete. Dynamo was leaderless: any replica could accept a write, conflicts were detected with vector clocks, and applications merged them. DynamoDB has one leader per partition that orders all writes through Multi-Paxos, so there are no conflicting versions to merge, and it offers strongly consistent reads served by the leader, with eventually consistent reads available per request.

The storage is different too. Dynamo used pluggable engines such as Berkeley DB or MySQL; each DynamoDB storage replica holds a write-ahead log and a B-tree of the data. And DynamoDB is a multi-tenant managed service with admission control, rather than an internal store run by one team.

The chapter flags this because the names cause confusion in design discussions. People sometimes attribute Dynamo's sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and application-level merging to DynamoDB. Those belong to the 2007 design and its descendants Cassandra and Riak. Architecturally, DynamoDB is a leader-based, consensus-replicated design (Multi-Paxos per partition), not a descendant of the original Dynamo's leaderless model.

quiz.q: Name two ways DynamoDB differs from the 2007 Dynamo design.
quiz.a: Any two: DynamoDB uses a Multi-Paxos leader per partition (Dynamo was leaderless); it offers strongly consistent reads (Dynamo was eventual with app merging); it stores data in B-trees; it is a managed multi-tenant service with admission control.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: DynamoDB's write path: quorum-persisted logs and fast log replicas
body: In DynamoDB, the partition leader keeps its role through a lease. A write is acknowledged once a quorum of replicas has persisted the write-ahead log record. Each storage replica holds a WAL and a B-tree of the data. Special log replicas hold only recent WAL entries: when a node fails, adding a log replica takes seconds, which restores the write quorum quickly. WALs are also archived to S3 for durability. A request router handles authentication and cached partition metadata lookups before forwarding requests.
deeper:
Acknowledging on WAL persistence rather than on B-tree updates keeps writes fast: appending a log record is sequential and cheap, and once a quorum has it, the write is durable even if the B-tree is updated later. This mirrors the single-node write-ahead logging pattern, lifted to a replicated setting.

Log replicas address a real availability problem. With three replicas and a majority quorum, losing one node leaves exactly two, with no margin. Rebuilding a full storage replica means copying the whole B-tree, which is slow. A log replica needs only recent WAL entries, so it can join in seconds and restore a comfortable write quorum while the full replacement is rebuilt in the background.

The lease lets the leader serve strongly consistent reads without consulting other replicas each time, since no other replica can become leader until the lease expires. Archiving WALs to S3 gives an additional durability layer beyond the three AZ replicas. Together these choices express the paper's theme of predictable performance even during failures.

quiz.q: Why does DynamoDB add log replicas when a storage node fails instead of only rebuilding a full replica?
quiz.a: A log replica holds only recent WAL entries, so it can be added in seconds to restore the write quorum, whereas copying a full B-tree replica takes much longer.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: DynamoDB's hot partition problem: throttled while under the limit
body: In DynamoDB's early design, a table's provisioned throughput was divided evenly across its partitions. A table with 4 partitions and 3,200 write units gave each partition 800. But real traffic is not even. One hot partition would be throttled while the others sat idle. Worse, when a partition split for size, each child got half the throughput, so customers saw throttling even though their table as a whole was under its limit. The chapter calls this the most useful lesson in the paper.
deeper:
The flaw was treating capacity as a property of partitions rather than of the table. Customers bought throughput for the table and reasonably expected to use all of it. But a skewed workload, where a few keys receive most traffic, concentrates load onto a few partitions, each capped at an even share.

Splits made it counterintuitive. As a table grew, DynamoDB split partitions to keep them a manageable size. Each split halved the per-partition throughput, so a growing table could become more likely to throttle hot keys over time, even with unchanged provisioning. From the customer's perspective, the database got worse as it grew.

The lesson generalizes beyond DynamoDB. Any system that divides a global budget evenly across shards will fail skewed workloads, and skew is the norm: celebrity users, popular products and large tenants appear everywhere. DynamoDB's fix came in stages: bursting, adaptive capacity, global admission control, and splitting for consumption, each addressing a weakness of the previous step, and each teaching something about handling skew.

quiz.q: Why did early DynamoDB customers see throttling even when their table was under its provisioned throughput?
quiz.a: Throughput was split evenly per partition, so a hot partition hit its small share while others were idle; splits halved per-partition throughput, making it worse as tables grew.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Bursting and adaptive capacity: DynamoDB's first two fixes
body: DynamoDB fixed hot partitions in stages. First came bursting: a partition could use unused capacity it had saved from recent idle periods. That helped short spikes only, because saved capacity runs out. Second came adaptive capacity: the system watched consumed versus provisioned capacity and raised the throughput of hot partitions in a throttled table. The paper says adaptive capacity eliminated over 99.99 percent of throttling due to skewed access, but it was reactive and best-effort.
deeper:
Bursting works like a bucket that fills while a partition is quiet. A brief surge can spend the saved credit without throttling. But a partition that is persistently hot has nothing saved, so bursting does nothing for sustained skew.

Adaptive capacity attacked sustained skew by moving budget toward partitions that needed it. The 99.99 percent figure shows how effective that was for the common case. Its weaknesses were in its nature. Being reactive, it only responded after throttling had begun, so customers still saw some errors while it adjusted. Being best-effort, it could not guarantee a hot partition would get enough, especially if the storage node hosting it was itself busy.

These limits pushed DynamoDB toward a design that removed the partition as the unit of admission altogether. That became global admission control, which tracks consumption at the table level so the per-partition budget question disappears. The progression illustrates a pattern: incremental fixes to a flawed abstraction help, but eventually the abstraction itself has to change.

quiz.q: Why did bursting help DynamoDB with short traffic spikes but not with persistently hot partitions?
quiz.a: Bursting spends capacity saved during recent idle periods; a persistently hot partition has no idle time to save credit, so there is nothing to spend.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Global admission control and split for consumption
body: DynamoDB's third fix was global admission control (GAC), which decoupled admission from partitions. Request routers take tokens from a GAC service that tracks a table's total consumption, so a table can use its full capacity even if traffic lands on few partitions. The fourth fix was split for consumption: when a partition stays hot, split it by key range, choosing the split point from the actual key distribution. Splits finish in minutes, spreading a hot range across more machines.
deeper:
GAC changes what capacity means. Instead of each partition enforcing its own slice, the table's budget is enforced in one place, at the routers, before requests reach storage. This matches customer expectations: if you bought 3,200 write units, you can spend them on whatever keys you like.

But admission alone does not add hardware. If one partition receives most of the traffic, the machine hosting it may still be overwhelmed.
