Split for consumption addresses that by physically dividing the hot key range so different machines share the load. Choosing the split point from actual key distribution matters: a naive midpoint split might leave nearly all hot keys on one side.

The method has explicit limits. Splitting does not help when one single item is hot, since an item cannot be divided, or when keys are accessed in sequence, since new traffic would simply move to the latest range. DynamoDB detects those patterns and does not split, avoiding pointless churn.

quiz.q: Why did DynamoDB still need split-for-consumption after global admission control?
quiz.a: GAC lets a table spend its full budget on any partitions, but a hot partition's machine can still be overloaded; splitting the hot range spreads the load across machines.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: No amount of partitioning fixes a single hot key
body: The permanent limit in DynamoDB's story is that splitting cannot fix a single hot item. One key lives on one partition, and it cannot be divided further. Sequential access patterns defeat splitting too, since new traffic keeps landing on the latest range. DynamoDB detects both patterns and declines to split. The lesson applies to every sharded database: if one key, such as a celebrity profile or a global counter, is too hot for one machine, you must fix it in the application or with a cache.
deeper:
This is why hot-key thinking belongs at design time. A shard key can spread billions of keys evenly and still fail if one key receives a disproportionate share of traffic. The database can move partitions around, admit requests globally and split ranges, but it cannot make one machine serve more than one machine's worth of requests for one item.

The remedies live above the database. A cache in front can absorb reads of the hot item. An application can split a logical item into several physical keys, for example spreading writes to a counter across multiple sub-keys and summing them on read. Sequential-key hot spots can be fixed by salting, hash-prefixing or reversing keys.

The chapter returns to this in its sharding section: a common mistake is choosing a shard key only for today's main query without asking what the hottest single key is and what happens when it grows 100 times. The senior staff design-review questions include the same point: what is the shard key, and what is the hottest single key?

quiz.q: Why can't DynamoDB split its way out of a single extremely hot item?
quiz.a: An item lives on exactly one partition and cannot be divided, so splitting ranges does nothing; the fix must come from the application (e.g. key splitting) or a cache.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Prime Day 2021: 89.2 million DynamoDB requests per second
body: In industry: during the 66-hour Prime Day event in 2021, Amazon systems made trillions of DynamoDB calls, peaking at 89.2 million requests per second, with single-digit millisecond latency. The number demonstrates DynamoDB's design goal of predictable performance at extreme scale. The chapter reports the figure as scale evidence; the design behind it is leader-based, Multi-Paxos replicated partitions, with global admission control and split-for-consumption so a table can use its full capacity without customers managing shards.
deeper:
The figure is notable for its latency as much as its throughput. Plenty of systems can reach high aggregate request rates if tail latency is allowed to balloon. Holding single-digit millisecond latency at 89.2 million requests per second is what the paper's goal of predictable performance looks like in practice.

That ties back to the hot partition story. Early DynamoDB divided throughput evenly across partitions, so skewed traffic throttled hot partitions. Bursting and adaptive capacity eased that; global admission control is what lets a table use its full capacity even when traffic lands on few partitions, and split-for-consumption spreads a persistently hot range across machines. (The chapter does not say which of these mattered on Prime Day.)

It also reflects a philosophy stated in the paper: design for predictability over absolute efficiency, and do not let caches hide work the system must be able to do without them. A system that only meets its latency targets with warm caches can collapse when caches go cold during a surge, which is exactly when a peak event needs it most.

quiz.q: What makes DynamoDB's Prime Day 2021 figure impressive beyond the raw 89.2 million requests per second?
quiz.a: It held single-digit millisecond latency at that peak, showing predictable performance rather than throughput bought with ballooning tail latency.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Predictability over efficiency: what happens when the cache is cold?
body: Senior staff lens: the DynamoDB paper has a line worth remembering. Design for predictability over absolute efficiency, and do not let caches hide work the system must be able to do without them. A cache can make a system look fast and cheap in normal operation while masking that the backend could not handle the real load alone. When reviewing a design, ask what happens when the cache is cold, for example after a restart, a failover or a sudden traffic shift.
deeper:
The danger is a hidden dependency. If a database normally serves 5 percent of requests because a cache absorbs the rest, the system is really sized for 5 percent. When the cache empties, the full load arrives at once, the backend overloads, requests time out, and the cache cannot refill because the backend is too busy. A brief cache problem becomes a long outage.

Predictability means the system behaves similarly in good and bad conditions. It may cost more hardware or accept slightly higher normal latency, but it avoids cliffs. DynamoDB's log replicas, which restore write quorums in seconds, and its global admission control fit the same philosophy: both reduce variance under failure and skew.

The principle applies directly to the chapter's other systems, many of which put caches in front of databases: Meta's TAO over MySQL and Uber's CacheFront over Docstore. The decision guide suggests a cache in front of user profiles. In each case, a reviewer should confirm the backing store can survive the cache being cold.

quiz.q: Why should a design review ask what happens when the cache is cold?
quiz.a: If the backend is only sized for cache misses, a cold cache sends full load to it, overloading it; predictable systems must be able to do the work without the cache.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Amazon Aurora: the log is the database (2017)
body: A normal MySQL instance on network-attached storage writes many things: data pages, redo log, binlog and a doublewrite buffer. With replicas in several zones, network I/O becomes the bottleneck. Aurora (2017 paper) fixes this by having the database engine, MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible, send only redo log records to storage. It never writes data pages over the network. A separate, multi-tenant storage fleet applies the redo records to build data pages itself, in the background and on demand.
deeper:
The insight is that redo log records are the minimal description of a change. Data pages, doublewrite copies and other artifacts can all be derived from the log. Sending only the log across the network removes most of the bytes a traditional database pushes to remote storage, which matters doubly when every write must be replicated to several zones.

Moving page construction into storage has a second benefit: crash recovery becomes almost instant. A traditional database must replay its redo log at startup to bring pages up to date. In Aurora, storage applies redo continuously, so there is little or nothing to replay when the engine restarts.

The results reported in the paper are striking. Aurora sustained 35 times more transactions than mirrored MySQL in a test, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction, even though it amplifies writes six ways by keeping six copies. It also streams continuous backup to S3. The design is often summarized as a scale-up SQL engine on top of a scale-out log.

quiz.q: Why does sending only redo log records to storage reduce Aurora's network I/O so sharply?
quiz.a: Redo records are the minimal description of changes; data pages, doublewrite copies and similar writes are derived from them by storage, so they no longer cross the network.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Aurora's 6-copy quorum: lose an AZ and keep writing
body: Aurora cuts the database volume into 10 GB segments. Each segment is copied 6 times into a protection group: two copies in each of three Availability Zones. Writes need 4 of 6 acknowledgments; reads during recovery need 3 of 6. So Aurora can lose a whole AZ, which takes two copies, and still write with the remaining four. It can lose a whole AZ plus one more node and still read with three, then rebuild its write quorum.
deeper:
The numbers are chosen so that write and read quorums always overlap: 4 plus 3 is 7, more than 6, so any read quorum includes at least one copy that saw the latest write.

Placing two copies per zone targets a specific failure model. Whole-AZ outages happen, and so do independent single-node failures. With two copies per AZ, losing an AZ removes exactly two copies, leaving four, enough to keep writing. If another node fails on top of that, three remain, enough to read and to repair, but not to write until a copy is rebuilt.

Segment size makes this safe in practice. A 10 GB segment can be repaired in about 10 seconds on a 10 Gbps link. Small segments mean the window during which a second or third failure could strike the same protection group is tiny, making double failures during repair very unlikely. Fast repair is as important to durability as the replica count.

quiz.q: Aurora keeps 6 copies with a 4/6 write quorum. What failures can it survive while still accepting writes?
quiz.a: It can lose an entire AZ (two copies) and keep writing with four; losing an AZ plus one more node still allows reads (3/6), then write quorum is rebuilt.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Small segments, fast repair, near-instant recovery in Aurora
body: Aurora splits storage into 10 GB segments so each can be repaired in about 10 seconds on a 10 Gbps link. Fast repair means the window for a second failure in the same group is tiny, making double failures very unlikely. Crash recovery is almost instant because storage already applies redo records continuously. The paper reports Aurora sustained 35 times more transactions than mirrored MySQL in a test, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction, despite amplifying writes six ways.
deeper:
The segment size is a durability decision disguised as a storage detail. Durability depends not only on how many copies exist but on how long the system stays degraded after a failure. If repairing a lost copy took hours, the chance of another failure hitting the same protection group during that time would be meaningful. Ten seconds shrinks that window to nearly nothing.

Continuous redo application removes the traditional recovery bottleneck. In a normal database, a crash means replaying potentially large amounts of redo log before the database can serve traffic. Aurora's storage is always applying redo in the background and can build pages on demand, so the engine does not wait for a long replay.

The performance paradox, six-way write amplification yet far fewer I/Os per transaction, resolves once you notice what is being multiplied. Aurora multiplies small redo records six ways, while mirrored MySQL multiplies full data pages, doublewrite copies, binlogs and redo logs across its mirrors. Six small writes beat many large ones.

quiz.q: How can Aurora do 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction than mirrored MySQL while keeping six copies of the data?
quiz.a: It replicates only small redo log records, while mirrored MySQL ships full data pages, doublewrite copies, binlog and redo across mirrors, so total I/O is far lower.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Aurora's limit: one writer, so it scales reads and storage, not writes
body: Aurora's classic design still has a single writer instance per cluster. All writes go through one machine running the SQL engine, so write throughput is limited to what one big machine can handle. Read replicas can read pages from the shared storage, and storage scales out across segments, but writes do not scale horizontally. The chapter calls this a "scale-up SQL with a scale-out log" design: it scales storage and reads, not writes.
deeper:
This limit is the price of Aurora's simplicity. With one writer, there is no need for distributed transactions, cross-shard coordination or a global clock; the engine behaves like ordinary MySQL or PostgreSQL, and applications keep full ACID semantics without change. The hard distributed-systems problems are confined to the storage layer, which only has to replicate and apply a log.

For many workloads, that is exactly the right trade. The chapter's decision guide recommends Aurora for money and orders when one writer is enough, and puts "Aurora or single MySQL/Postgres plus replicas" on the branch where multi-row ACID transactions are needed and writes fit one big primary.

When writes do not fit one machine, the options change. Spanner-style NewSQL systems such as Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB split the data into consensus-replicated ranges with distributed transactions, and Vitess shards MySQL when per-shard ACID is enough. Those give write scalability at the cost of distributed coordination.

quiz.q: When should a team pick Aurora over a Spanner-style NewSQL database for transactional data?
quiz.a: When multi-row ACID is needed but write volume fits one big primary; Aurora scales reads and storage, not writes, while avoiding distributed-transaction complexity.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Meta's UDB and MyRocks: same MySQL, 62.3% smaller
body: Meta keeps its core social data in MySQL. Its main database, UDB (User Database), holds tens of petabytes of likes, comments, shares and other social graph data. When UDB moved from spinning disks to flash, the bottleneck moved from IOPS to capacity. InnoDB had three space problems: index fragmentation, weak compression and 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead. Meta built MyRocks, a MySQL storage engine on RocksDB, so applications could keep using MySQL while storing data more compactly.
deeper:
The UDB migration finished in 2017. Results: instance size 62.3 percent smaller than compressed InnoDB, 75 percent fewer bytes written, and fewer than half as many UDB servers. At tens of petabytes, halving the server count is an enormous saving.

The strategy was to change the engine without changing the interface. Applications, tooling and operational knowledge built around MySQL stayed the same; only the layer that lays bytes on disk changed. That is possible because the storage engine sits beneath SQL and replication, which mostly do not care how it works.

Each InnoDB problem maps to an LSM advantage. Fragmentation from half-full B-tree pages disappears because SSTables are packed full. Weak compression improves because sorted, full files compress better than individually compressed pages with free space. The chapter lists InnoDB's 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead as the third problem MyRocks was built to escape. Fewer bytes written also extends SSD life, reinforcing why the chapter calls LSM the winner on capacity once flash is in place.

quiz.q: What three InnoDB problems did MyRocks address for Meta's UDB, and why did they matter after moving to flash?
quiz.a: Index fragmentation, weak compression and 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead; on flash the bottleneck became capacity, so wasted space was the main cost.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: TAO: Meta's graph-aware cache over MySQL (2013)
body: Reading Meta's social graph straight from MySQL, or through memcache, was hard to keep consistent and efficient. TAO (2013) is a graph-aware cache and API over MySQL. It models data as objects, such as users and posts, and associations, which are typed edges such as "likes" or "friend". It is a two-level cache: follower tiers serve clients, and a leader tier per shard talks to the database and sends invalidations to followers. All writes to a shard go through its leader.
deeper:
Understanding the data shape is what makes TAO effective. A generic key-value cache stores opaque blobs, so the application must manage graph relationships and invalidation itself, and that is where inconsistency creeps in. TAO knows about objects and associations, so it can cache edge lists and update them correctly when an association is added or removed.

The two-tier structure separates scale from correctness. Follower tiers can be replicated widely to absorb enormous read fan-out. The leader tier for each shard is the single path to the database for writes, so it can order updates and tell followers which cached entries to invalidate. The chapter's comparison table describes TAO's consistency as eventual, with read-after-write within a tier.

TAO was reported to handle a billion reads and millions of writes per second in 2013. It is read-mostly by design, matching a social graph where content is viewed far more than it is created. Chapter 6 returns to TAO's caching side.

quiz.q: Why does routing all of a shard's writes through a TAO leader help keep caches consistent?
quiz.a: The leader orders the shard's writes to MySQL and sends invalidations to follower tiers, so there is one place that knows about each change and can update caches correctly.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: ZippyDB: Meta's strongly consistent key-value store on RocksDB
body: Before ZippyDB (first deployed 2013), many Meta teams used RocksDB directly, and each rebuilt replication and failover on its own. ZippyDB is a general-purpose, strongly consistent key-value store that does this once. It uses RocksDB as the engine, Data Shuttle (a Multi-Paxos replication library) for replication, and ShardManager for placing shards. It offers per-request consistency: each request can ask for eventual, read-your-writes, or strong consistency, trading latency for freshness as needed.
deeper:
Sharding is layered. Physical shards are about 50 to 100 GB, and each holds tens of thousands of micro-shards (μshards). The Akkio mapping moves μshards between regions to keep data near its users. Moving small μshards is far cheaper and finer-grained than moving whole physical shards, so data can follow users without large migrations. This follows the resharding pattern of creating many small logical shards from the start.

Per-request consistency is a practical design. Strong reads must go through the Paxos leader and may cross regions; eventual reads can be served by any nearby replica. Read-your-writes sits between: a client sees its own updates without paying for global strong consistency on every read. Letting the caller choose avoids forcing one expensive guarantee on every workload.

The broader motivation is platform consolidation. When many teams each build replication and failover on a raw engine, each repeats the same hard work and the same bugs. Netflix later reached a similar conclusion about Cassandra and built a key-value abstraction layer.

quiz.q: Why did Meta build ZippyDB instead of letting teams keep using RocksDB directly?
quiz.a: RocksDB is a single-node library; each team was rebuilding replication and failover on it, so ZippyDB provided those once as a shared, strongly consistent service.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Meta's recipe: keep MySQL, swap the engine, add a smart cache
body: In industry: Meta's pattern is "keep the relational store, change the engine, and put a smart cache in front". MySQL plus MyRocks provides durability and transactions for core social data. TAO, a graph-aware cache, handles graph reads at huge fan-out. ZippyDB covers simple key-value needs with strong consistency options. Rather than replacing MySQL with a new database, Meta improved what sat beneath it and in front of it, and built separate stores for needs MySQL did not fit.
deeper:
The pattern avoids a risky rewrite. Moving tens of petabytes of social data to a brand-new database would mean new query semantics, new tooling and years of migration risk. Changing only the storage engine to MyRocks kept the MySQL interface and operational practices while delivering large space and write savings.

The cache layer addresses the access pattern MySQL handles worst: enormous read fan-out over graph relationships. TAO turns those reads into cache hits with graph-aware invalidation, leaving MySQL as the durable source of truth.

ZippyDB fills a different gap: workloads that just need a replicated key-value store, which previously led teams to wire RocksDB up themselves.

The chapter's key takeaways generalize this: Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of their storage engines. For Meta it is TAO; for LinkedIn, Espresso routers; for Uber, the Docstore query engine; for Netflix, its key-value abstraction. The engine is reused; the layer in front is where each company differentiates.

quiz.q: Why did Meta change MySQL's storage engine rather than migrate its social data to a new database?
quiz.a: It kept the familiar MySQL interface, tooling and transactions while gaining LSM space and write savings, avoiding the risk of migrating tens of petabytes to new semantics.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: LinkedIn Espresso: the document store that replaced Oracle
body: Espresso, introduced publicly in 2015, is LinkedIn's primary document store. It replaced Oracle for many applications because of license cost, hardware cost and painful schema changes. Stateless routers hash the partition key and forward requests. Storage nodes use MySQL/InnoDB as the local engine and keep documents as Avro binaries with JSON schemas. Apache Helix manages cluster state: which node is master for which partition, failover and rebalancing. In 2015 it powered about 30 applications and held hundreds of terabytes.
deeper:
Espresso shows the chapter's layered pattern clearly. The single-node engine is ordinary MySQL/InnoDB. Everything distinctive lives around it: routing, partitioning, cluster management and change capture.

Databus, LinkedIn's change-capture system, streams changes for replication and for downstream consumers. That lets search indexes, caches and analytics pipelines follow the primary data without querying it directly.

The data model has four levels: database, table, collection and document. Secondary indexes are local, one per partition. A local index is cheap and consistent to update because it lives on the same partition as the data, but any query by an indexed field not scoped to one partition must ask every partition, the scatter-gather cost discussed in the secondary index section.

At its 2015 scale, Espresso served millions of records per second at peak and held hundreds of terabytes before replicas. The comparison table lists it as a document store with strong consistency per partition via its master, replicated master-slave with Helix and Databus, on InnoDB.

quiz.q: What roles do Apache Helix and Databus play in Espresso?
quiz.a: Helix manages cluster state (which node masters each partition, failover, rebalancing); Databus captures and streams changes for replication and downstream consumers.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: LinkedIn Venice: a store for data you can always rebuild
body: Venice, open-sourced in 2022, is LinkedIn's derived data platform. Derived data is computed by batch or stream jobs, for example ML features or "people you may know" results. Its source of truth lives elsewhere, so Venice optimizes for bulk loading and fast reads, not transactions. Writes arrive as full dataset pushes from Hadoop, or as nearline updates from Samza, through Kafka. Storage nodes use RocksDB, and the Da Vinci client can keep a local copy of a dataset inside the application.
deeper:
Venice's scale numbers show how large derived data gets. By 2018 it had replaced about 500 Voldemort read-only use cases. The 2022 post reported more than 1,800 datasets, more than 300 applications, peak ingest of 50 GB per second, and 6.25 million single-get queries per second at peak.

The write path fits the data's nature. A batch job that recomputes recommendations produces a whole new dataset, so Venice accepts full pushes and swaps them in, which the comparison table describes as eventual consistency with bulk swap. Nearline updates from stream processing cover changes between full pushes. Kafka carries both, decoupling producers from storage nodes.

The Da Vinci client takes read speed to its limit: by keeping a local copy inside the application process, reads avoid the network entirely. That is only reasonable because the data is derived and read-mostly; staleness of a few moments is acceptable and the copy can always be rebuilt.

RocksDB's LSM design suits bulk loading and compact storage, making it a natural engine choice here.

quiz.q: Why can Venice skip per-write transactional guarantees that a primary database needs?
quiz.a: Its data is derived from sources stored elsewhere, so it can always be recomputed and reloaded; losing a write is recoverable, letting it favor bulk loads and fast reads.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Primary data and derived data need different stores
body: Senior staff lens: Venice shows a pattern many teams miss. Primary data and derived data need different stores. Primary data is the source of truth, such as a user's profile or a payment. Its store needs durability of each write, transactions and backups. Derived data, such as ML features or recommendations computed from primary data, can be rebuilt from its inputs, so its store can trade per-write durability for bulk loads and read speed.
deeper:
Putting both kinds of data in one store forces bad compromises. Loading a freshly computed 50 GB dataset through a transactional database's per-write path wastes effort on guarantees the data does not need and competes with the latency-sensitive primary workload. Conversely, putting primary data in a store optimized for bulk swaps risks losing records that cannot be regenerated.

Separating them lets each be tuned properly. The primary store invests in replication, write-ahead logging and backups. The derived store invests in bulk ingest, compact storage and fast reads, and recovers from failure by rerunning the job that produced it.

This distinction appears as the first question in the chapter's five design-review questions: what is the source of truth, and can this data be rebuilt? It also shows up in the decision guide, which assigns ML features and precomputed results to a derived-data store like Venice, and bulk-loaded derived data to a Venice-style store as one of the main branches of the decision tree.

quiz.q: What property of derived data lets its store trade per-write durability for bulk loads and read speed?
quiz.a: It can be rebuilt from its inputs by rerunning the batch or stream job, so losing some writes is recoverable, unlike primary source-of-truth data.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Uber Docstore: MySQL partitions replicated with Raft
body: Uber's first scalable datastore, Schemaless (2016), was an append-only layer on top of sharded MySQL. In 2021 Uber described how it evolved into Docstore, a general-purpose distributed SQL-like database. A stateless query engine layer routes requests. A storage engine layer organizes data into partitions, each with 3 to 5 nodes in independent zones running MySQL, replicated with Raft. Uber wraps MySQL transactions as the unit that Raft replicates, giving strict serializability within a partition.
deeper:
Replicating whole MySQL transactions through Raft is an elegant combination. MySQL provides a proven local engine with transactions; Raft provides consensus replication across zones. Each partition behaves as a single strictly serializable database replicated to 3 to 5 nodes, so losing a zone does not lose committed data.

Docstore adds features on top: schemas, transactions, materialized views, and change data capture through Flux, which tails the MySQL binlog. Change capture lets other systems react to data changes without polling the database.

Its 2021 scale was tens of millions of queries per second, 99.99 percent or better availability, and tens of petabytes of operational data. In 2024 Uber added CacheFront, a Redis cache built into the Docstore query engine and kept fresh by Flux, serving over 40 million reads per second. Building the cache into the query engine, and invalidating it from the change stream, keeps applications from managing cache consistency themselves. Chapter 6 covers CacheFront in detail.

quiz.q: How does Docstore get strict serializability within a partition while replicating across zones?
quiz.a: Each partition runs MySQL on 3 to 5 nodes in separate zones, and Uber replicates whole MySQL transactions through Raft, so every replica applies the same ordered transactions.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Uber's Cassandra fleet: tens of thousands of nodes, real pain points
body: Uber also runs large Cassandra fleets for workloads that need high write throughput and TTLs (data that expires). Its 2023 post described tens of thousands of nodes, hundreds of clusters of 6 to 450 nodes each, tens of millions of queries per second, and petabytes of data. The main operational pain points were unreliable node replacement, lightweight-transaction errors, and slow anti-entropy repair, which Uber fixed by building a repair scheduler inside Cassandra.
deeper:
Uber runs both Docstore and Cassandra because they fit different workloads. Docstore gives transactions and strict serializability per partition on MySQL. Cassandra's leaderless LSM design gives very high write throughput and native TTL support, suited to data such as time-ordered events that expire.

The pain points are instructive because they come from Cassandra's Dynamo heritage. In a leaderless system, replicas can diverge, so anti-entropy repair is needed to reconcile them, the job Dynamo did with Merkle trees. At tens of thousands of nodes, repair that is slow or poorly scheduled leaves data inconsistent for long periods and consumes resources. Building the scheduler inside Cassandra made repair routine rather than an external chore.

Node replacement is a constant at this scale: with tens of thousands of machines, some are always failing, so replacing them must be reliable and automated. Lightweight transactions, Cassandra's compare-and-set feature built on consensus, add coordination to a system otherwise designed to avoid it, which is where errors can appear.

quiz.q: Why does a leaderless system like Cassandra need anti-entropy repair, and why is it hard at Uber's scale?
quiz.a: Replicas accept writes independently and can diverge, so repair must reconcile them; at tens of thousands of nodes, slow repair leaves inconsistency and eats resources.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Cassandra: Dynamo's ring plus Bigtable's storage
body: Apache Cassandra came out of Facebook in 2008, originally for inbox search. It combines Dynamo's leaderless ring, meaning consistent hashing, tunable consistency and hinted handoff, with Bigtable's LSM storage: a commit log, memtable and SSTables. That combination makes it very good at high write rates across many datacenters, because any replica can accept writes and LSM writes are sequential. It is weak at transactions and ad-hoc queries, since there is no leader to coordinate and data must be modeled around its keys.
deeper:
Each half of the design contributes something. From Dynamo comes availability: no leader to fail over, writes accepted by whichever replicas are reachable, and per-request consistency levels that let an application trade freshness for latency. From Bigtable comes efficient storage: memtable plus commit log for fast durable writes, immutable SSTables, and compaction strategies such as size-tiered and time-window.

The weaknesses follow from the same choices. Without a leader, coordinating multi-row transactions is difficult. Without a global index, queries must be designed around partition keys; Cassandra's classic secondary indexes are local, so a query on an indexed column asks every node.

The chapter lists Cassandra at Uber, Apple, Netflix and Instagram, with tunable, eventual consistency, leaderless ring replication and LSM storage. The decision guide places Cassandra, along with Bigtable and HBase, on the branch for write-heavy, time-ordered data such as messages and feeds keyed by user and time bucket.

quiz.q: What does Cassandra take from Dynamo and what from Bigtable?
quiz.a: From Dynamo: the leaderless ring with consistent hashing, tunable consistency and hinted handoff. From Bigtable: LSM storage with commit log, memtable and SSTables.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Apple's 75,000 nodes and Instagram's Rocksandra
body: Apple stated around 2015 that it ran over 75,000 Cassandra nodes storing more than 10 PB, and it is a major contributor to the project. Instagram began using Cassandra in 2012 and describes one of the world's largest deployments. In 2018 it built Rocksandra, which swaps Cassandra's Java storage engine for RocksDB. The goal was to cut tail latency caused by Java garbage collection, where the runtime pauses to reclaim memory and slow requests stack up.
deeper:
Apple's numbers show how far the leaderless LSM design can scale in node count. At 75,000 nodes, the absence of a central leader or master for the data path is an advantage: there is no single component that every request must pass through.

Instagram's problem was latency, not capacity. Garbage-collected languages periodically pause to reclaim memory. For a storage engine juggling many objects for memtables, caches and compaction, those pauses show up as occasional very slow requests, raising p99 latency even when averages look fine. Moving the storage engine into RocksDB, written in C++ with explicit memory management, removed that source of pauses while keeping Cassandra's distribution layer.

Rocksandra is a small-scale version of the chapter's recurring theme. Just as Meta put RocksDB under MySQL and TiKV and YugabyteDB built on it, Instagram kept the distributed layer it knew and replaced only the single-node engine. The engine is a reusable component; the distribution layer carries the company-specific value.

quiz.q: Why did Instagram replace Cassandra's storage engine with RocksDB in Rocksandra?
quiz.a: Cassandra's Java engine suffered garbage-collection pauses that caused tail latency; RocksDB's C++ engine avoids those pauses while Cassandra's distribution layer stays.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Netflix's Key-Value abstraction: stop every team repeating mistakes
body: Netflix manages petabytes of data in Cassandra. Over time it found that each team using Cassandra directly repeated the same mistakes: poor data modeling, large partitions and unsafe retries. Its answer, described in a 2024 post, was a Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer on its internal Data Gateway platform. Applications call a simple key-value API, a map of id to a sorted map of items, and the platform handles the backing store, mostly Cassandra, plus features like chunking large values and idempotency tokens for safe retries.
deeper:
The abstraction encodes hard-won lessons once instead of relying on every team to learn them. Large partitions, where too much data accumulates under one partition key, hurt Cassandra performance; chunking large values and a constrained data model help avoid them. Retries after timeouts can apply a write twice; idempotency tokens let the platform recognize a repeated request and apply it only once.

The simple API shape, id mapped to a sorted map of items, covers many common patterns, such as a user's list of events sorted by time, while hiding Cassandra-specific details. That also gives Netflix freedom: because applications no longer talk to Cassandra directly, the platform can change or tune the backing store without application changes.

This mirrors Meta's reason for ZippyDB and belongs to the chapter's broader takeaway. Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of their storage engines. The engines are shared or open source; the layer in front is where each company captures its operational knowledge.

quiz.q: What problem was Netflix's Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer meant to solve?
quiz.a: Teams using Cassandra directly kept repeating the same mistakes (data modeling, large partitions, retries); the layer gives a simple API and handles those concerns once in the platform.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Vitess: YouTube moved sharding out of the app into a proxy
body: Vitess was built at YouTube starting in 2010 to scale MySQL. YouTube had gone from one primary, to read replicas, to application-level sharding, and the sharding logic in application code was getting painful. Vitess moved it into a proxy layer. VTGate is a stateless proxy that speaks the MySQL protocol, parses queries and routes them to the right shard. VTTablet is a sidecar next to each MySQL instance adding connection pooling, query safety limits and health checks.
deeper:
The remaining components complete the system. A topology service, etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, stores which shards exist and where. Vindexes define how a row's column maps to a shard: by hash, through a lookup table, and so on. Lookup vindexes are an example of directory partitioning, where a mapping table decides placement.

Because VTGate speaks the MySQL protocol, applications connect as if to a single MySQL database. The routing, which used to be scattered through application code, lives in one place that can be upgraded and operated independently.

VTTablet's safety features matter at scale. Connection pooling protects MySQL from floods of client connections, and query limits stop a runaway query from harming a shard.

Online resharding is the other key feature: Vitess splits a shard by copying data with filtered binlog replication, then switching traffic. This is the online copy-and-cutover approach to resharding. Vitess graduated from the CNCF in November 2019.

quiz.q: Why was moving sharding logic from application code into VTGate valuable?
quiz.a: Applications connect to one MySQL-protocol endpoint while routing lives in a single proxy layer, so sharding logic is no longer scattered and painful to change in app code.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: Slack on Vitess: 2.3 million queries per second at 11 ms p99
body: Slack originally sharded MySQL by workspace. Large customers created hot shards, and features like cross-workspace channels did not fit the model, since one channel's data spanned workspaces on different shards. Slack began moving to Vitess in 2017. By December 2020, 99 percent of Slack's MySQL traffic ran on Vitess, peaking at 2.3 million queries per second, 2 million reads and 300,000 writes, with 2 ms median and 11 ms p99 latency.
deeper:
Slack's original scheme was tenant grouping with a directory: each workspace lived on one shard, found through a mapping. That is attractive because most operations stay inside one workspace and therefore one shard. Its weaknesses appeared as the product grew. A very large workspace concentrated load on one shard, the hot-tenant problem. Cross-workspace channels broke the assumption that all related data lived together.

Vitess moved sharding into a proxy layer with vindexes that define how rows map to shards, and its online resharding (filtered binlog replication, then a traffic switch) let data be redistributed while the system kept running. VTGate made the change largely transparent to application code, because it still spoke the MySQL protocol.

The migration took from 2017 to late 2020 to reach 99 percent, showing that resharding a live, large system is slow even with good tooling. The chapter's common-mistake box makes the same point: a bad shard key is the most expensive decision to undo in a database, and Slack's workspace key had to be undone for features the original design did not anticipate.

quiz.q: What two problems pushed Slack away from sharding MySQL by workspace?
quiz.a: Large customers created hot shards, and cross-workspace channels did not fit a model where each workspace's data lived on one shard.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: NewSQL: CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB copy Spanner
body: NewSQL means distributed databases that keep SQL and ACID transactions but scale horizontally. The three popular open ones follow the Spanner pattern. CockroachDB speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, stores data in ranges replicated by Raft, with a leaseholder serving reads and writes, on the Pebble LSM engine. TiDB is MySQL compatible, with stateless TiDB servers over TiKV regions replicated by Raft (3 replicas by default) on RocksDB. YugabyteDB offers YSQL (PostgreSQL compatible) and YCQL over Raft-replicated tablets on DocDB, built on RocksDB.
deeper:
What they share is the Spanner blueprint. The key space is sorted and split into ranges of a few hundred MB. Each range is a consensus group. A transaction layer on top coordinates multi-range writes. Ranges split and move automatically, so capacity grows without manual resharding.

The names differ, range, region, tablet, but the unit is the same idea as Spanner's Paxos groups, using Raft instead of Paxos. All three also put an LSM engine at the bottom, either RocksDB or the RocksDB-inspired Pebble, another sign that RocksDB is the engine inside the engine.

TiDB adds TiFlash, a columnar replica for analytics, so analytical queries can run on a copy of the data laid out by column without disturbing the transactional row store.

In the comparison table, these systems offer serializable or snapshot consistency with Raft per range. The decision guide lists them alongside Spanner for workloads that need multi-row ACID transactions but whose writes do not fit one big primary.

quiz.q: What architecture do CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB share with Spanner?
quiz.a: A sorted key space split into ranges of a few hundred MB, each a consensus (Raft) group, with a transaction layer for multi-range writes and automatic split and move.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
title: NewSQL's real difference: how each system gets its clock
body: The open NewSQL systems differ mostly in how they order transactions in time. TiDB uses a central timestamp oracle in its Placement Driver (PD): one service hands out timestamps. That is simple and correct but adds a round trip to one service. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use hybrid logical clocks instead, avoiding a central service. The price is that they must bound clock skew between machines and sometimes retry reads that fall in the uncertainty window.
deeper:
The problem they are all solving is the one Spanner solved with TrueTime: making timestamps from different machines comparable so transactions appear in a consistent order. Spanner uses GPS and atomic clocks to keep uncertainty to a few milliseconds and waits it out. None of the open systems assume that hardware.

A central oracle sidesteps clock uncertainty entirely: if one service issues every timestamp in increasing order, ordering is trivially correct. The cost is a network round trip to that service for transactions, and the service must be highly available.

Hybrid logical clocks combine each machine's physical clock with a logical counter, keeping timestamps close to real time while preserving causal order. Because physical clocks can disagree, the system assumes skew stays under a configured maximum. When a read finds a value whose timestamp is too close to its own to be sure which came first, it cannot know the true order, so it retries at a later timestamp. That occasional retry is the price of having no central clock service.

quiz.q: Compare TiDB's timestamp oracle with CockroachDB's hybrid logical clocks.
quiz.a: TiDB's central oracle is simple and correct but adds a round trip to one service; hybrid logical clocks avoid a central service but must bound clock skew and sometimes retry uncertain reads.

title: Hash partitioning: even load, but range scans hit every shard
body: Sharding, or partitioning, splits data across machines, and every large system does it. Hash partitioning assigns shard = hash(key) mod N, or places keys on a consistent-hash ring. Hashing scatters keys evenly, so load is balanced and sequential keys do not create a hot range. The downside is that neighboring keys land on different shards, so a range scan across keys has to hit every shard. Dynamo, Cassandra, DynamoDB (on the partition key) and Espresso use hash partitioning.
deeper:
The choice between plain modulo and a consistent-hash ring matters when the cluster changes size. With hash(key) mod N, changing N moves almost every key to a new shard, forcing a huge reshuffle. A consistent-hash ring moves only the keys adjacent to added or removed nodes, which is why Dynamo used it, with virtual nodes to smooth out load.

Even spreading protects against a whole class of hot spots. Timestamps and auto-increment IDs, which would pile onto the last range under range partitioning, are scattered across all shards by hashing.

But hashing only spreads different keys. A single hot key still lands on one shard, the limit DynamoDB's paper stresses. And any query that is not a lookup by the full hash key, such as "all orders between two dates", must fan out to every shard. Systems like DynamoDB and Cassandra partly address this by hashing only a partition key and keeping rows within a partition sorted by a secondary key, so scans inside one partition stay cheap.

quiz.q: Why does hash partitioning avoid hot spots from sequential keys but make range scans expensive?
quiz.a: Hashing scatters consecutive keys across all shards, spreading load evenly, but that means a range of keys lives on every shard, so a range scan must query them all.

title: Range partitioning: cheap scans, but new keys all hit one shard
body: Range partitioning gives each shard a contiguous key range, like a dictionary split into volumes. Range scans are cheap because adjacent keys sit together on one shard, and splits are natural: when a range grows too big, cut it in two. The weakness is sequential keys. If keys are timestamps or auto-increment IDs, every new write goes to the last range, creating a hot tail. Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB, TiKV and HBase use range partitioning.
deeper:
Range partitioning suits systems that sort data by key, which is why it pairs naturally with LSM-trees and B-trees whose data is already ordered. Bigtable's tablets, Spanner's tablets, CockroachDB's ranges and TiKV's regions are all contiguous key ranges that split automatically as they grow, making resharding largely an automatic background process.

The hot-tail problem is the flip side of cheap scans. Because nearby keys share a shard, keys that arrive in order all hit the same shard. Splitting does not help: after a split, new keys still go to the newest range. DynamoDB's split-for-consumption explicitly detects sequential access and declines to split for this reason.

The chapter's fix is to change the key: salt it, hash-prefix it, or reverse it so that new writes spread across ranges. Bigtable's reversed-URL example shows reversal used to group related data; the same trick applied to sequential IDs spreads writes. The trade-off is that scans in the original key order become harder.

quiz.q: Why doesn't automatic splitting fix the hot spot created by auto-increment keys in a range-partitioned system?
quiz.a: After a split, every new key is still larger than all existing ones, so writes keep going to the newest range; the hot spot just moves with the tail.

title: Directory partitioning: a lookup table decides where each key lives
body: Directory, or lookup, partitioning uses a mapping table that says where each key or tenant lives. It is the most flexible pattern: you can move one big customer to its own shard without touching anyone else, because moving just means updating the directory entry. The cost is an extra hop to consult the directory, and the directory itself must be highly available and cached, since every request depends on it. Slack's original workspace mapping, Vitess lookup vindexes and Meta's Akkio for μshards use it.
deeper:
Flexibility is the reason to accept the extra hop. Hash and range schemes compute placement from the key, so moving an individual key means changing the function for everyone. A directory records placement explicitly, so any key or tenant can be placed anywhere. That makes it well suited to multi-tenant systems with very uneven tenants, where a few giants need dedicated capacity.

Meta's Akkio shows another use: moving μshards between regions to keep data near its users. Because placement is looked up rather than computed, a μshard can follow a user who moves.

The directory's weaknesses are operational. It is on the path of every request, so if it is slow or down, everything is. It must be replicated for availability and cached for speed, and the caches must be kept consistent with moves. Slack's experience also shows the limits of tenant-level directories: mapping whole workspaces to shards let large customers create hot shards, and data that spanned tenants, such as cross-workspace channels, did not fit.

quiz.q: What makes directory partitioning the most flexible sharding pattern, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Placement is recorded per key or tenant, so any one can be moved just by updating the mapping; the cost is an extra lookup hop and a directory that must be highly available and cached.

title: Entity grouping: keep one user's data together, skip cross-shard work
body: Entity or tenant grouping keeps all the data of one user or one workspace together on the same shard. The goal is that most transactions touch only one entity, so they stay inside one shard and avoid expensive distributed transactions. Spanner does this with interleaved tables and directories: related rows, such as a customer and their orders, share a key prefix and are stored and moved together. Grouping works alongside the other patterns, deciding what should live together rather than how keys are spread.
deeper:
Cross-shard transactions are the most expensive operation in a distributed database. They need coordination such as two-phase commit, which adds round trips and latency. If a user's profile, settings and orders all live together, updating several of them atomically is a local transaction on one shard.

Spanner's directories are the concrete mechanism. A directory is a set of keys with a common prefix, and it is the unit Spanner moves between Paxos groups; a 50 MB directory can be moved in a few seconds. Interleaving child tables under a parent row keeps the parent and children in the same directory, so they always move together.

The risk is uneven entity sizes. An entity that grows very large, such as a giant tenant or a celebrity user, can outgrow one shard and become a hot spot. Slack's workspace-based sharding showed this: most workspaces fit comfortably, but large customers created hot shards, and data spanning workspaces did not fit. Good designs ask upfront how large the biggest entity can grow.

quiz.q: Why does grouping all of one user's data on the same shard make transactions cheaper?
quiz.a: Transactions that touch only one user's data stay on a single shard and run locally, avoiding distributed coordination like two-phase commit across shards.

title: Resharding tip: create thousands of small logical shards on day one
body: Resharding, changing how data is split across machines, is where teams get hurt. One proven approach is many small logical shards from day one. For example, create 4,096 logical shards spread over 16 machines. When you need more capacity, you move whole logical shards to new machines instead of re-hashing individual rows. The mapping from key to logical shard never changes; only the mapping from logical shard to machine does. ZippyDB's μshards and Redis's 16,384 hash slots follow this idea.
deeper:
The trick separates two mappings. Key to logical shard is fixed by a hash function and never changes, so no row ever needs to be reassigned by recomputation. Logical shard to machine is a small table that can change freely. Growing from 16 to 32 machines just means moving half the logical shards, with each move being a bounded copy of one unit.

Compare that with hash(key) mod N on physical machines: changing N from 16 to 17 reassigns almost every key, which means a massive, risky data migration. Small logical shards turn resharding into routine rebalancing.

The number of logical shards is chosen once and must be large enough for future growth, since it sets the maximum number of machines you can spread across without further splitting. Choosing thousands leaves room. ZippyDB layers this further, with physical shards of about 50 to 100 GB each holding tens of thousands of μshards, and Akkio moving μshards between regions. Redis Cluster's fixed 16,384 hash slots are the same pattern in a widely used open-source system.

quiz.q: Why does creating 4,096 logical shards on 16 machines make later growth easier than hashing directly to machines?
quiz.a: The key-to-logical-shard mapping never changes, so growth only moves whole logical shards between machines instead of re-hashing and reassigning individual rows.

title: Resharding options: automatic splits or online copy and cutover
body: Besides many small logical shards, two other resharding approaches exist. Automatic split and merge of ranges, used by Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB and DynamoDB, is best for operators because the system reshapes itself, but it needs a system built for it from the start. Online copy and cutover, used by Vitess and most MySQL shops, copies data to new shards, keeps them in sync with replication or change data capture, verifies, then flips routing. It needs a short write pause or careful double-writes.
deeper:
Automatic splitting works when the database owns routing and placement end to end. Range-partitioned systems can cut a range in two, hand one half to another server and update metadata, all without application involvement. Retrofitting that onto a system not designed for it is very hard, which is why it is a from-the-start choice.

Online copy and cutover is the practical path for existing databases such as sharded MySQL. The steps are: create the new shards, bulk copy existing data, stream ongoing changes (Vitess uses filtered binlog replication), verify that old and new match, and switch routing to the new shards. The hardest moment is the switch. Writes arriving during the flip could land on the old shard after copying finished, so teams either pause writes briefly or write to both old and new locations during the transition.

Slack's multi-year migration to Vitess shows the effort involved even with good tooling, reinforcing the chapter's advice: plan for resharding from day one, because the shard key is among the hardest decisions to undo.

quiz.q: Why does online copy-and-cutover resharding need a short write pause or double-writes?
quiz.a: Writes arriving during the routing flip could land on the old shard after copying, so they must be paused briefly or written to both old and new shards to avoid loss.

title: Common mistake: picking a shard key for today's query only
body: Common mistake: choosing a shard key only for today's main query. Before committing, also ask: what is the hottest single key, such as a celebrity user or a giant tenant? What happens when it grows 100 times? Will most transactions stay in one shard? A shard key that looks fine for current traffic can create hot shards or force cross-shard transactions as the product evolves. A bad shard key is the most expensive decision to undo in a database.
deeper:
The shard key determines where every row lives, so changing it later means moving essentially all data, rewriting routing, and often changing application logic that assumed the old grouping. That is why it is harder to undo than an index or a schema field.

Each question targets a known failure. The hottest single key matters because no sharding scheme can split one key; DynamoDB's paper makes this the permanent limit. Growth by 100 times matters because skew compounds: a tenant that uses 1 percent of a shard today may overflow it later. Transaction locality matters because cross-shard transactions are slow and complex; if common operations span shards, the key is wrong.

Slack is a real example. Sharding by workspace served its early product, but large customers created hot shards and cross-workspace channels did not fit, leading to a Vitess migration that began in 2017 and reached 99 percent of MySQL traffic by December 2020. The chapter's design-review questions repeat the point: what is the shard key, and what is the hottest single key?

quiz.q: Name the three questions to ask about a shard key beyond whether it fits today's main query.
quiz.a: What is the hottest single key (celebrity or giant tenant), what happens when it grows 100 times, and will most transactions stay within one shard?

title: Common mistake: timestamps as the leading part of a range key
body: Common mistake: using a timestamp or auto-increment ID as the leading part of a range-partitioned key. Because range partitioning keeps adjacent keys together, and every new timestamp or ID is larger than the last, all new writes go to one range: the newest one. That single shard becomes a hot spot while the rest of the cluster idles. The fix is to salt the key, hash-prefix it, or reverse it, so new writes spread across many ranges.
deeper:
Each fix breaks the correlation between arrival order and key order. Salting adds a small random or computed prefix, such as one of 16 bucket numbers, so consecutive writes land in 16 different ranges. Hash-prefixing puts a hash of some field, such as the user ID, at the front of the key, spreading writes by user while keeping each user's rows together and sorted by time. Reversing, as in Bigtable's reversed URLs, changes which part of the key varies first.

The cost is on the read side. A query for "everything in the last hour" now must check every salt bucket or every hash prefix instead of scanning one range. Good designs choose the leading key part that matches the dominant access pattern. The chapter's decision guide does exactly this for messages and feeds: key them by (user_id, time bucket), so writes spread across users while one user's recent messages remain a cheap scan.

Automatic splitting does not rescue a sequential key, because the hot tail simply moves to the newest range after each split.

quiz.q: How does keying messages by (user_id, time bucket) avoid the timestamp hot-spot problem?
quiz.a: Leading with user_id spreads new writes across many ranges by user, while time within each user keeps that user's recent messages together for cheap scans.

title: Local secondary indexes: cheap writes, scatter-gather reads
body: A secondary index lets you find rows by a column other than the primary key, for example finding a user by email. In a sharded database, a local index, also called document-partitioned, means each shard indexes only its own rows. Writes are cheap and consistent, because the row and its index entry live on the same shard. But a query by the indexed column must ask every shard and combine the results, called scatter-gather. Tail latency grows with the number of shards.
deeper:
Local indexes are the natural default because they require no coordination. When a row changes, its index entry on the same shard changes in the same local transaction, so the index is never stale. Cassandra's classic secondary indexes and Espresso's per-partition indexes work this way.

The cost appears on reads. A query like "find the user with this email" does not know which shard holds the user, so it goes to all of them. The work grows linearly with shard count, and worse, the query's latency is set by the slowest shard to respond. As shard count grows, the chance that at least one shard is slow approaches certainty, so the query's typical latency becomes the shards' tail latency.

Local indexes are therefore best for queries that are already scoped to one partition. If data is partitioned by user, an index on message time within each user's partition serves "messages of this user sorted by time" from a single shard, with no scatter-gather at all.

quiz.q: Why are writes to a local secondary index cheap and always consistent?
quiz.a: The row and its index entry live on the same shard, so both are updated together in one local transaction, with no cross-shard coordination.

title: Global secondary indexes: one lookup, but writes cross shards
body: A global secondary index, also called term-partitioned, is its own sharded table keyed by the indexed value. To find a user by email, you look up the email in the index shard that owns it, then read the row: one lookup instead of asking every shard. The catch is writes. Updating a base row must also update an index row that usually lives on a different shard. That requires either a distributed transaction or an asynchronous update that leaves the index briefly stale.
deeper:
The two write strategies map to real systems. Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB update global indexes within a distributed transaction, so the index is always consistent with the data. The price is that every write touching an indexed column becomes a multi-shard transaction, with the extra round trips and latency that implies.

DynamoDB's global secondary indexes take the other path: they are updated asynchronously and are eventually consistent. Writes stay fast and single-partition, but a query through the index may briefly miss a recent change or return an old value.

Neither is free; the question is which cost the application can tolerate. For a login lookup by email, a slightly slower signup write may be fine, while a briefly stale index might be acceptable for search. The chapter's advice is to make this choice explicit in the API contract, so callers know whether an index read can be stale. The index's own sharding also matters: a very popular indexed value can still become a hot key on one index shard.

quiz.q: What are the two ways to keep a global secondary index updated, and what does each cost?
quiz.a: Synchronously via distributed transaction (consistent, but slower multi-shard writes, as in Spanner/CockroachDB/TiDB) or asynchronously (fast writes, briefly stale index, as in DynamoDB GSIs).

title: Why fanning out to 200 shards makes p99 your typical latency
body: Back-of-envelope: with 200 shards and a local index, a "find by email" query fans out to all 200. If each shard is slower than its own p99 (99th percentile latency) 1 percent of the time, the chance that at least one of 200 shards is that slow is 1 - 0.99^200, about 87 percent. So the query's typical latency is roughly the shards' p99. A global index avoids this: it needs one index lookup plus one read.
deeper:
The math reveals why scatter-gather scales badly even when every shard is healthy. A query that waits for all shards is as slow as the slowest one. Rare slowness per shard becomes common slowness per query once enough shards are involved: at 200 shards, 87 percent of queries hit at least one slow shard. At 500 shards, as in the chapter's quiz, the query latency approaches the worst shard's tail almost every time.

This has cost implications too. Each fanned-out query consumes resources on every shard, so a high volume of such queries multiplies total load by the shard count, even though only one shard holds the answer.

The global index turns the problem around: two targeted requests, each subject only to its own shard's latency distribution. The trade is on the write side, where the index update is either a distributed transaction or asynchronous. The lesson generalizes beyond indexes: any request that must wait for many servers inherits their tail latency, so fan-out should be limited on hot paths.

quiz.q: You must support "find user by email" across 500 shards. Compare a local index and a global index for this query.
quiz.a: Local: cheap writes, but every query hits all 500 shards and latency approaches the worst shard's tail. Global: one index lookup, but user writes must update another shard, synchronously or asynchronously.

title: Pick index type by query volume, and state staleness in the API
body: Senior staff lens: for high-volume lookups by a non-key field, prefer a global index or a separate lookup table. Accept that it is either slower to write (synchronous update) or briefly stale (asynchronous update), and make that explicit in the API contract so callers know what to expect. Keep local indexes for queries that are already scoped to one partition, for example "messages of this user sorted by time" in a database partitioned by user.
deeper:
The guidance follows from where each index type pays. A local index pays on every cross-partition read; a global index pays on every write. For a lookup that runs constantly, such as finding a user by email at login, paying on reads across hundreds of shards is ruinous, while paying once per write is affordable. For a query that naturally names its partition, a local index costs nothing extra on reads and stays perfectly consistent.

A separate lookup table is the manual version of a global index: the application maintains a mapping from, say, email to user ID. It gives the same single-lookup reads and the same write-side choice between synchronous and asynchronous updates.

Making staleness explicit is the part teams skip. If an asynchronous index can lag by seconds, a user who just changed their email might not be found by the new one. Stating that in the API lets callers design around it, for example by reading the primary row after a write. The decision guide applies this directly: user profiles get a global email index plus a cache.

quiz.q: When should you keep a local index rather than build a global one?
quiz.a: When queries are already scoped to one partition, such as a user's messages sorted by time in a user-partitioned store, since the local index then serves them from one shard with consistent writes.

title: The big comparison: where each system puts consistency
body: Across the chapter's systems, consistency ranges widely. Bigtable is single-row atomic. Spanner offers external consistency via Paxos and TrueTime. Dynamo is eventual with app-merged conflicts, while DynamoDB offers strong or eventual reads per request. Aurora is ACID with a single writer. TAO is eventual with read-after-write in a tier; ZippyDB is tunable per request. Espresso is strong per partition via its master; Docstore is strict serializable per partition. Venice is eventual with bulk swap; Cassandra tunable and eventual; NewSQL serializable or snapshot.
deeper:
The table also shows the engines underneath. LSM storage: Bigtable (SSTables), Cassandra, and RocksDB in MyRocks, ZippyDB and Venice, with Pebble or RocksDB under CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB. B-trees: Spanner's B-tree-like files on Colossus and DynamoDB. InnoDB: Espresso, Docstore and Vitess. Aurora uses a log-structured storage service; Dynamo had pluggable engines (Berkeley DB, MySQL); TAO sits on MySQL.

Replication styles cluster into a few families: consensus per group (Spanner's Paxos, DynamoDB and ZippyDB's Multi-Paxos, Docstore and NewSQL's Raft), leaderless quorums (Dynamo, Cassandra), quorum storage (Aurora's 6 copies with 4/6 writes), file-system replication (Bigtable via GFS/Colossus), primary-replica MySQL (MyRocks, Vitess, Espresso via Helix and Databus), and Kafka-based pipelines (Venice).

Scale evidence spans 60+ products (Bigtable, 2006), trillions of rows by design (Spanner), 89.2 million requests per second (DynamoDB, Prime Day 2021), 35x mirrored MySQL in test (Aurora), tens of petabytes (UDB, Docstore), 1 billion reads per second (TAO), 6.25 million gets per second (Venice), and 2.3 million QPS (Slack on Vitess).

quiz.q: Which systems in the comparison offer strong consistency only within a partition, and why is that a common choice?
quiz.a: Espresso and Docstore (strong per partition), plus Vitess and MySQL+MyRocks (ACID per shard). Keeping strong guarantees inside one partition avoids costly cross-partition coordination.

title: One company, five databases: matching stores to data
body: Using the running example of a 1-billion-user app, one company ends up with several databases. User profiles, read-heavy and looked up by email, go in sharded MySQL (Vitess, Docstore or Espresso-like) or DynamoDB, with a global email index and a cache in front. Money and orders need cross-row transactions: Spanner-style NewSQL, or Aurora if one writer is enough. Messages and feeds, write-heavy, time-ordered and TTL'd, fit Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase keyed by (user_id, time bucket).
deeper:
Two more categories complete the set. The social graph belongs in a graph cache like TAO over a durable relational store, because graph reads have enormous fan-out and are far more common than writes. ML features and precomputed results belong in a derived-data store like Venice, since they can be rebuilt from their inputs and benefit from bulk loads and fast reads.

The reasoning in each case ties back to earlier sections. Profiles need point lookups by a non-key field, so they get a global index rather than scatter-gather over a local one, and a cache for read volume, subject to the rule of asking what happens when the cache is cold. Money needs multi-row ACID, so it goes where transactions are native. Messages need high write throughput and expiry, so they go to LSM-based stores with time-oriented compaction, keyed to avoid the timestamp hot tail. The graph gets Meta's pattern. Derived data gets the primary-versus-derived split.

No single database is best at all of these, which is why large companies run several.

quiz.q: Why does the decision guide key messages and feeds by (user_id, time bucket) in Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase?
quiz.a: The data is write-heavy, time-ordered and expiring, which suits LSM stores; leading with user_id spreads writes across shards while keeping each user's recent messages together.

title: The decision tree: ACID first, then access pattern
body: For a new structured dataset, first ask: do you need multi-row ACID transactions? If yes, ask whether writes fit one big primary. If they do, use Aurora or a single MySQL/Postgres with replicas. If not, use Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB or YugabyteDB, or Vitess if per-shard ACID is enough. If you do not need multi-row ACID, choose by access pattern: key lookups with predictable latency (DynamoDB, ZippyDB, Espresso-like), write-heavy time-ordered scans (Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase), or bulk-loaded derived data (Venice-style).
deeper:
The tree front-loads the most expensive requirement. Multi-row ACID transactions constrain the choice more than anything else, so it comes first. Within that branch, write volume decides between scale-up and scale-out: one big primary avoids distributed transactions entirely, which is simpler and faster, and should be preferred when it fits. Only when writes exceed one machine is it worth paying for consensus-replicated ranges and distributed commit. Vitess is the middle option when transactions can be confined to a shard.

Without multi-row ACID, the access pattern dominates. Predictable point lookups favor leader-based key-value or document stores with good partitioning and admission control. Write-heavy, time-ordered data with scans favors LSM-based wide-column stores. Data computed elsewhere favors a derived-data store optimized for bulk loads.

The tree is a starting point, not an algorithm to follow blindly. It captures the chapter's core trade-offs: consistency versus scale, B-tree versus LSM, and primary versus derived data. The senior staff questions refine the choice further.

quiz.q: In the decision tree, why pick Aurora or a single primary over Spanner-style NewSQL when writes fit one big machine?
quiz.a: One primary avoids distributed transactions and consensus overhead, giving simpler operation and lower write latency; NewSQL's cost is only worth paying when writes exceed one machine.

title: Five design-review questions that pick the database for you
body: Senior staff lens: in a design review, ask five questions. First, what is the source of truth, and can this data be rebuilt? Second, what is the shard key, and what is the hottest single key? Third, which reads must see the latest write? Fourth, how do we add capacity without downtime? Fifth, what is the blast radius when one shard, one zone or one region is lost? The answers usually pick the database for you.
deeper:
Each question compresses a lesson from the chapter. Source of truth separates primary from derived data, as Venice showed: rebuildable data can live in a bulk-loaded store without per-write durability. The shard key and hottest key reflect DynamoDB's permanent limit and Slack's costly workspace sharding. Which reads need the latest write decides between strong consistency, per-request consistency as in ZippyDB and DynamoDB, synchronous versus asynchronous global indexes, and cache freshness.

Adding capacity without downtime points at resharding strategy: many small logical shards, automatic range splits, or online copy and cutover, chosen from day one rather than retrofitted. Blast radius covers replication design: Aurora survives losing an AZ, DynamoDB replicates across three AZs, Spanner can span regions, and shard-level failures should affect only a fraction of users.

Together the questions shift attention from product names to requirements. Once you know what can be rebuilt, what is hot, what must be fresh, how growth happens and what failure looks like, the right system is usually obvious.

quiz.q: Why does asking "can this data be rebuilt?" help choose a database?
quiz.a: Rebuildable (derived) data can live in a store optimized for bulk loads and fast reads without per-write durability; source-of-truth data needs durable writes, transactions and backups.

title: Chapter recap: engines, compaction and RocksDB
body: The storage engine sets the per-node cost of reads, writes and space. B-trees favor reads and in-place updates. LSM-trees favor writes and space, and pay with compaction and read amplification. Compaction strategy is a workload decision: leveled saves space, tiered saves write bandwidth, FIFO fits TTL data. RocksDB is the shared engine under much of the industry, including MyRocks, ZippyDB, Venice, TiKV and YugabyteDB. Companies differentiate in replication and sharding, not in the single-node engine.
deeper:
These points form the foundation layer of the chapter. The RUM conjecture frames the engine choice: read, write and space amplification cannot all be minimized, so B-trees and LSM-trees simply sit at different points of the trade-off. Meta's MyRocks migration is the proof that the choice matters at scale: 62.3 percent smaller instances, 75 percent fewer bytes written, and fewer than half as many UDB servers once flash made capacity the bottleneck.

Compaction is where LSM designs live or die. Leveled compaction keeps space overhead near 11 percent with a 10x multiplier but rewrites data once per level. Tiered compaction rewrites less but keeps overlapping files and may need double space during merges. FIFO drops whole files for expiring data. Undersizing disk bandwidth for compaction leads to Level 0 backlog, slower reads and write stalls.

RocksDB's ubiquity follows from economics: a correct, fast, crash-safe LSM engine takes years to build and need not differ between companies, so the industry reuses it and invests in the distributed layers above.

quiz.q: Summarize the B-tree vs LSM trade-off in one sentence each.
quiz.a: B-trees favor reads and in-place updates, paying with page-sized writes and fragmentation; LSM-trees favor writes and space, paying with compaction work and read amplification.

title: Chapter recap: distributed designs, sharding and indexes
body: Bigtable separated serving (tablet servers) from durability (GFS/Colossus). Spanner added Paxos groups and TrueTime for external consistency, paying with write latency. Dynamo (2007) was leaderless and eventually consistent; DynamoDB (2022 paper) uses Multi-Paxos leaders, B-trees and global admission control, and splitting cannot fix a single hot item. Aurora sends only redo records to a 6-way, 3-AZ storage service with 4/6 write quorums, scaling storage and reads, not writes. The shard key and index choice are hardest to undo.
deeper:
A further pattern runs through the company case studies: Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of the storage engines. For Meta it is TAO over MySQL; for LinkedIn, Espresso's routers; for Uber, the Docstore query engine; for Netflix, the Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer. Those layers hold each company's operational knowledge: routing, caching, safe retries, data modeling rules.

The final takeaway is about irreversibility. The shard key and the choice between global and local secondary indexes are the hardest decisions to undo, because changing them means moving or re-indexing all data. Plan for the hottest key, since no partitioning scheme can split one key, and plan for resharding from day one, using many small logical shards, automatic range splits or online copy and cutover.

The consistency question posed at the start of the case studies ties everything together: each system chose where to put consistency, from single-row atomicity to external consistency, and gave something up, usually latency, write scalability or query flexibility, to get scale.

quiz.q: Why are the shard key and the global-vs-local index choice considered the hardest database decisions to undo?
quiz.a: Changing either means redistributing or re-indexing all existing data and often changing application assumptions, unlike most tuning choices that can be adjusted in place.
